articles.title: Democratic lawmakers face backlash after consecutive legislative missteps
articles.summary: Fresh off their midterm victories, Democrats are already facing a postelection reality check. In the span of two days, Democrats stumbled on two major fights, with some members missing a critical procedural vote on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and the party failing to call for a recorded vote on a GOP veterans bill they…
articles.body:
Fresh off their midterm victories, Democrats are already facing a postelection reality check.

In the span of two days, Democrats stumbled on two major fights, with some members missing a critical procedural vote on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and the party failing to call for a recorded vote on a GOP veterans bill they argued would expand some benefits while cutting others.

The back-to-back missteps prompted one Democratic lawmaker to deliver a blunt assessment: The party needs to lock in.

“It was two f‑‑‑ ups in two days,” the lawmaker, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, told The Hill.

“I think what it means is that we all need to get out of celebration mode and into back-to-work mode. And I think that’s really it. I mean, you know, kind of coming off of this high of having these incredible election results, all of the new members here this week. There’s a lot of excitement, a lot of celebrating, a lot of parties, and all that. But we’ve got a job to do, and hopefully, these two very unfortunate incidents are a reminder to everyone that we need to do that job,” that lawmaker added.

The blunders have blemished what was supposed to be a week of triumph and celebration for Democrats following their landslide midterm victories that will give them roughly 260 seats in the next Congress.

The errors have also put the spotlight on the Democrats’ leadership team — particularly Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) and Katherine Clark (D-Mass.), the minority whip — just as they prepare to take control of the majority, raising questions about well how they will govern the caucus.

A second Democrat compared the missteps to mistakes made recently by the Commanders, Washington’s NFL team, which has drawn vitriol for a string of self-inflicted mistakes this season that’s left them near the bottom of their division.

“I’m pretty sure they’re just anomalies, but we’ve [got] to tighten that up,” said the lawmaker, who spoke anonymously to discuss a sensitive topic. “And I guess that’s Katherine’s lane, but Hakeem’s taking the hit for it. And I get it. He is the captain of the ship.”

“But that stuff shouldn’t happen — and definitely when we get in control next year, we can’t afford misses like that,” the lawmaker added. “That’s the stuff [Mike] Johnson and [Kevin] McCarthy got in trouble for.”

Asked about the blunders on Thursday, Jeffries punted, shifting the topic to note that Democrats had succeeded in forcing their veterans’ benefits bill to the floor, where it passed easily.

A third Democratic lawmaker said that leadership needs to make sure Democrats “are prepared for every single situation.”

“The floor is, you know, the whip, but I think the entire leadership team has to be clear with people that we’re done celebrating, in that we can’t celebrate at the expense of the floor,” the lawmaker said.

For months, Democrats have railed against Hegseth, accusing him of waging an “illegal” war in Iran and demanding his ouster. But when they finally had a chance to advance a resolution to impeach him, 11 Democrats missed Tuesday’s vote. House Republicans voted to send the resolution to committee by a vote of 211-204, effectively burying the effort.

Some Democrats, including Reps. Jonathan Jackson (Ill.) and Melanie Stansbury (N.M.), said they were stuck in a traffic jam and couldn’t make it to the House floor on time. Former Speaker Nancy Pelosi’s (D-Calif.) office said she was at a Veterans Day event in San Francisco, while Nevada Democrat Steven Horsford cited a “personal emergency.”

During a meeting Wednesday morning, Clark told Democrats they had disappointed the American people by having absences on the vote, according to a source who was inside the room.

Then, on Wednesday, Democrats faced another beating. Despite whipping against the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act (TCAVA), no member on the Democratic side demanded a roll-call vote.

Democrats accused Republicans of playing “dirty pool,” alleging that they pulled House Veterans’ Affairs Committee ranking member Rep. Mark Takano (D-Calif.) away from the podium to ask if he would agree to “last minute engrossment corrections.” While he was away, they argued, the Republican lawmaker presiding over the House chamber called up a voice vote.

A GOP aide disputed that argument, noting that Democrats botched normal procedure and did not have a member ready at the mic to call for a recorded vote, thus leading the bill to be adopted by a voice vote. The aide noted that engrossment corrections are taken up after a bill has passed.

Still, the third Democratic lawmaker said Democrats need to be ready for “Republican trickery.”

“We have to be ready for all of their — they’re going to play hardball. We need to play hardball back. We have a job to do here, and I think that, you know, we should anticipate what they might do and be ready for it and be ready to take it on because I do think that what they did with the bill yesterday was, I mean, they played dirty. We should know that, so we got to be ready to take it on,” the second lawmaker said.

The first lawmaker said “it’s going to be a very hectic couple of months” even before Democrats take control in January.

“We know that there is a very full agenda that the Republicans are going to try to clear before the end of this Congress, right? We’re going to do government funding, defense bill, FISA [Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act], probably permitting, right? It’s going to be very busy. And then on top of that, all of the preparation of, you know, making sure that we are ready to come out of the gate strong with an agenda of good bills when we take the majority in November. So, like, I think for a lot of members on the Democratic side, like a lot of members are already locked in and focused on that work. But … everybody else needs to pull it together and get focused,” the lawmaker said.

Some Democrats have said the two incidents this week are not an indication that the party is in disarray or that Jeffries is struggling to manage his conference as leader. Jeffries is expected to be the Speaker next year.

“Let’s talk about the people who missed the impeachment vote. That was an unforced error. Should have never happened. Members know that they’re supposed to be on the floor with their votes,” a fourth lawmaker said.

“They know that traffic in D.C. can be unpredictable. Just inexcusable. Not disarray. It was just one of those weird circumstances. And as it relates to the procedural thing, it was a trick of the Republicans to sneak that in. You just don’t do that. … Now we weren’t on our game and we let it get by,” the lawmaker added.

“We can always do better at making sure we’re organized,” the lawmaker said.

A fifth Democratic lawmaker, meanwhile, argued that “Republicans are in disarray.”

“They just had historic losses because of the toxic nature of the policies that they pursue. So I think that’s where the focus should be,” the lawmaker said.

Rep. Jim McGovern (D-Mass.), who’s in line to chair the powerful Rules Committee, acknowledged that Democrats should have been present to vote for Hegseth’s impeachment and they should have been more vigilant in demanding a recorded vote on the GOP’s veterans bill. But he also suggested Republicans were less than forthright in fast-tracking that proposal — and Democrats will be more wary in the remaining weeks of the lame-duck session.

“If this is the new approach of the Republicans during the last weeks of their power that they’re going to, like, whisper into the microphone so that no one knows what the hell they’re doing, then we’re just going to have to be on high alert,” McGovern said.

articles.title: GOP senators warn Trump push for Pentagon funding risks shutdown
articles.summary: Republican senators are warning President Trump’s aggressive push for GOP leaders to use the budget reconciliation process to ram $350 billion in spending for the Defense Department through Congress could risk a government shutdown next month. Senators in both parties say a deal is coming together behind the scenes to fund the federal government past…
articles.body:
Republican senators are warning President Trump’s aggressive push for GOP leaders to use the budget reconciliation process to ram $350 billion in spending for the Defense Department through Congress could risk a government shutdown next month.

Senators in both parties say a deal is coming together behind the scenes to fund the federal government past the looming Dec. 11 deadline, but they warn those negotiations would be spoiled by an effort to use the budget reconciliation process to dramatically increase Pentagon funding during the Iran war.

Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) warned that pushing a budget reconciliation package in the lame-duck session “absolutely” would increase the risk of a government shutdown.

He warned that attempting to increase defense funding by using reconciliation, a special process that would allow Republicans to circumvent a Democratic filibuster, would make negotiations on a broader government funding deal more difficult.

“That’s just hiding from the fact that they would simply subtract whatever you did in reconciliation from what they otherwise would agree to do in regular appropriations,” he said.

“Whatever you put into reconciliation, I think [Democrats] would take out of appropriations,” he predicted.

He said that would make it “very difficult” to reach a deal to avoid an end-of-year government shutdown.

Rounds said if Republicans negotiate in good faith on a stopgap government funding measure, Democrats would agree to a deal.

Trump isn’t willing to accept a smaller Pentagon budget next year and is pressing Republicans to use the budget reconciliation process to increase the Pentagon budget with party-line votes.

The president on Thursday called on Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) to “IMMEDIATELY move” a budget reconciliation package to provide $350 billion in supplemental funding to the Defense Department.

“The Radical Democrat Majority in the next Congress has already made it clear that their Number One Agenda is to BLOCK and RESIST this historic investment in our National Security,” Trump posted on Truth Social.

“That’s why TODAY I am calling on Senate Leadership to IMMEDIATELY move on the 350 Billion Dollar Reconciliation Bill to give our brave Warriors the DECISIVE ADVANTAGE they deserve,” he posted.

Republicans used budget reconciliation last year to pass the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and again this year to fund Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection through 2029.

But Senate Republicans, still smarting from the loss of at least eight seats in last week’s election — losses they blame on Trump’s unpopularity — are pushing back.

“The White House is still wanting to go it alone and we saw what that got us 10 days ago. I think we’ve got to come up with a different way,” said Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), noting Democrats’ sweeping victories in Senate and House races last week.

Tillis argued using the budget reconciliation process once again to pass huge spending bills without any Democratic support would be a mistake unless Democrats refuse to agree to any “reasonable” government funding deal and leave Republicans no other option.

“I’ve been saying this to my colleagues: Guys, we got to be reasonable.”

He warned that if Republicans move immediately to force defense funding through Congress by using the budget reconciliation process, it could trigger another shutdown — the third of Trump’s second term.

“I think it could” increase the chances of a shutdown, he said.

Tillis argued Republicans probably can’t get enough votes to advance a budget reconciliation package, given divisions within their ranks on both sides of the Capitol.

“There’s a lot of impediments to getting a reconciliation, just agreeing on what the bounds would be,” he said.

He said his preference would be to fund the Defense Department and the rest of the government with bipartisan support.

Senate Democrats have already warned Thune that if Republicans ram through extra Pentagon funding through the budget reconciliation process, it would imperil a deal to avoid a shutdown.

Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) warned “any kind of tricks or gimmicks certainly threatens a potential agreement.”

Asked if Republicans moving a budget reconciliation package would “poison the well” for striking a deal on government funding next month, Sen. Mark Warner (D-Va.) replied: “Yes.”

A senior Democratic aide said moving supplemental defense funding through the budget reconciliation process would undermine the chances of reaching a funding deal next month.

Right now, leaders in both parties are eyeing a short-term funding deal to keep federal departments and agencies operating into April.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) doesn’t want the funding fight over fiscal 2027 to intrude on the first 100 days of the new Democratic House and Senate majorities.

A Republican senator who requested anonymity to comment on internal discussions said Thune has privately discouraged Republican colleagues from pushing a partisan reconciliation package in the lame-duck session.

“Thune has been discouraging on reconciliation,” the source said. “I think the priority is judges, which you’re seeing here, and government funding. That’s what Thune has outlined as the must-do’s.”

Senate Republicans expect they will confirm another 23 of Trump’s judicial nominees — four circuit court nominees and 19 District Court nominees — before relinquishing the majority to Democrats.

Thune has told colleagues that Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) has warned Senate Republican leadership that he doesn’t think he can get the votes he needs to send it to the Senate.

Thune told reporters he’s open to moving a budget reconciliation package to fund the Defense Department but isn’t sure if he or Johnson could muster the votes to pass it.

“We’re having some discussions and conversations around the subject, but no decisions yet,” he said. “It’s what you can get 50 votes for here and 218 in the House.”

He said the chairs and ranking members of the Senate and House Appropriations committees have begun negotiations to keep the government funded into next year.

“We’re getting into that discussion, but we got to keep the government funded, for sure,” he said.

articles.title: 6 Gen Z federal and state officials you should know
articles.summary: Generation Z representation will triple in the next Congress after last week’s midterms, as Rep. Maxwell Frost (D-Fla.) will be joined by Rep.-elect Melat Kiros (D-Colo.) and Rep.-elect Michael Alfonso (R-Wis.). Gen Z makes up just 2.5 percent of the new class in the 120th Congress, and millennials make up 40 percent. But their numbers…
articles.body:
Generation Z representation will triple in the next Congress after last week’s midterms, as Rep. Maxwell Frost (D-Fla.) will be joined by Rep.-elect Melat Kiros (D-Colo.) and Rep.-elect Michael Alfonso (R-Wis.).

Gen Z makes up just 2.5 percent of the new class in the 120th Congress, and millennials make up 40 percent . But their numbers are growing with last week’s elections. Frost was the only Gen Zer in the 119th Congress, and millennials made up just 16 percent of the group.

Congress also gained record-breaking numbers of young lawmakers, who won 102 races this election cycle, per Future Caucus .

The Gen Z candidates represented both political parties, signaling different kinds of voters may have been attracted to younger candidates.

Amanda Litman, co-founder and president of Run For Something, an organization that recruits progressive candidates to run for office across the nation, said 36 of their Gen Zers won races.

“I think so many people running this year, they were talking about affordability. They were in particular talking about housing. They were talking about transportation. They were talking about transparency,” Litman told The Hill. “Many of them were talking about their personal experiences growing up in working class families.”

“It’s not that they won on identity, but their lived experiences really shaped how they talk about the issues,” she added.

Litman believes that Gen Z candidates — and Gen Zers in office — are uniquely good communicators.

“Elected officials who are really effective communicators can better connect with their voters,” she said. “They’re also often more honest, more transparent about the challenges that they face as they govern.”

Here are six names to watch as Congress and a number of state houses get a little more Gen Z.

Kiros, a 29-year-old democratic socialist, will represent Colorado’s 1st District as the first female Gen Zer in Congress. She won more than 78 percent of the vote , easily beating out Republican Christy Peterson and independent Shimon Blau.

Kiros defeated 15-term incumbent Rep. Diana DeGette (D-Colo.) in the Democratic primary, and she’s signaling that she’s ready to shake things up.

“Democrats won back Congress on a promise to fight corruption. Keeping that promise means setting a high standard of transparency for ourselves,” Kiros wrote in a Nov. 6 post on the social platform X. “A meeting about our party’s future belongs in full view of the press.”

Like many new Democrats headed to Washington, D.C., Kiros has been particularly critical of the war in Gaza, the role corporate PAC money plays in politics and current Democratic leadership.

In July, the representative-elect told The Hill’s Drew Petrimoulx, “I look forward to having conversations with [House] Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries about what the direction of our party should be and making sure we are disentangling ourselves from a lot of this special interest corporate PAC money, but this is a rule that I’m going to have for leadership writ large.”

She echoed that sentiment earlier this week in a response to a post from fellow Democratic Rep.-elect Richard Ojeda (N.C.), who wrote, “ Get big money out of politics . Period.”

“No more excuses, let’s get it done,” Kiros replied Monday.

Alfonso, a Republican, became the youngest elected member of Congress at 26 years old. He secured 56 percent of the vote in Wisconsin’s 7th Congressional District against Democrat Fred Clark to succeed Rep. Tom Tiffany (R).

Alfonso has close ties to the Trump administration as the son-in-law of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, who held the same seat from 2010 to 2019.

Alfonso received a degree from University of Wisconsin-Madison and became a major voice for Gen Z Republicans, especially with his support of late political commentator Charlie Kirk and Turning Point USA.

“Gen Z is shifting right in record numbers. More conservative. More Christian. But Washington doesn’t represent them right now. In the wake of Charlie Kirk’s assassination, Michael Alfonso is stepping up to fight for the next generation of Americans, their values, and their future,” his campaign website reads.

Alfonso doubled down in an interview with local television station WSAW , saying that “Republicans have not achieved everything” when it comes to the administration’s goals so far.

“What have been the cornerstones of your campaign thus far?” WSAW news anchor Kassandra Sepeda asked Alfonso in an October interview.

“There are three — affordability, affordability, affordability,” Alfonso responded. “One of the really unique things I think I bring to the table is a perspective on housing,” referencing his time spent working on construction projects in the area and how much it costs to build a home.

Rep.-elect Houston Gaines (R), a 31-year-old from Athens, Ga., is set to succeed Rep. Mike Collins (R-Ga.), 59, who gave up his seat to run for Senate.

Gaines clinched an endorsement from President Trump to represent Georgia’s 10th Congressional District and campaigned on cracking down on illegal immigration, supporting law enforcement, cutting government spending and lowering taxes.

“Whether it’s the cost of living and housing, our national debt, advancements in technology, or the future of education, these sort of issues will shape our generations for decades to come,” Gaines said in a statement to The Hill.

He’s part of a generational shift of 30-somethings who emerged as front-runners in their races, per the Atlanta Journal-Constitution . He first won a seat in the Georgia House of Representatives in 2018 when he was 23 years old. In his tenure, he said he authored more than 20 bills that became law.

He said that it’s important to have the next generation in leadership because of the unique viewpoint it brings.

“My goal is to bring a fresh perspective, get things done, and help make sure the next generation has the same opportunities to succeed that generations before us have enjoyed,” Gaines added. “I also hope to show that young people can make a real difference in government.”

State rep.-elect Ella Barrett (D), 22, was elected as part of a wave of new Gen Z representatives in New Hampshire’s legislature.

The state house flipped from red to blue last week, partly driven by 12 new Gen Z candidates winning their races.

Barrett argued she represents change in that she’s like the people who elected her, while casting too many state lawmakers as being wealthy and out of touch.

“A lot of our representatives are independently wealthy or retired. It’s more difficult for young folks to run for office,” she told The Hill. Barrett will make $100 per year in her new role while substitute teaching and living at home.

Barrett, a recent graduate of Mount Holyoke College, said that she was surprised on the campaign trail when people reacted with excitement to her age.

“People were really excited that there was someone new, someone young and someone with energy at their door, willing to talk and listen,” she said.

State rep.-elect Claire Lynn (R-Ore.) is a 27-year-old who is now among the youngest Republican women to serve in the Oregon House, per the Oregon Capital Chronicle .

“I understand what it’s like to be building a career, planning for the future and trying to get ahead in a state where the cost of living continues to rise,” she told The Hill. “These aren’t just issues my husband and I hear about. They’re challenges we’re navigating ourselves.”

A seventh-generation Oregonian who worked in D.C. on Capitol Hill and in the state legislature, she expressed excitement about being a younger voice pushing against the “status quo.”

Tyler Smith (D), the newly elected Texas state representative, will be the Lone Star State’s first Gen Z Democrat to serve in the state House.

“I think the issues that matter most from education to healthcare to the environment to the economy, those are all issues that will impact my generation to come,” Smith told The Hill on Thursday. “And I’m happy that the state of Texas, that the people of Texas are giving us [Gen Z] a voice at the table, because it’s needed.”

Smith was born in Houston, grew up in Los Angeles and moved back home to attend Texas Southern University.

The 26-year-old Democrat ran on high-priority issues for his generation, including lowering housing and healthcare costs, keeping criminals off the streets and fixing the state’s power grid.

“In order for us to keep this momentum with Gen Z voters and young voters, we have to keep up on the promises we made as a party,” Smith said.

He believes November’s wave of Gen Z and millennial politicians on the state and national level is an opportunity to get more younger people into politics.

“We have a strong opportunity to get more younger faces and younger voices involved as we see this shift in generational policies and politics,” Smith said.

The Feed is a weekly scoop on Generation Z put together by three Generation Z editors at The Hill. We’re working to understand the ins and outs of our generation’s politics. Send tips or comments to awalker@thehill.com , jfeldstein@thehill.com or cleibowitz@thehill.com .

articles.title: Feijóo, sobre el servicio militar: “No quiero llegar a eso porque conllevaría un problema de seguridad máximo”
articles.standfirst: El líder del PP considera que Europa atraviesa una situación crítica por las amenazas en sus fronteras
articles.summary: El líder del PP considera que Europa atraviesa una situación crítica por las amenazas en sus fronteras
articles.body: Alberto Núñez Feijóo ha descartado promover la recuperación del servicio militar obligatorio en España si llega a la presidencia del Gobierno. El presidente del Partido Popular ha abordado esta posibilidad durante su entrevista en el pódcast de Jordi Wild, donde ha explicado que no contempla dar ese paso en el actual contexto, aunque ha advertido de los riesgos de seguridad que afronta Europa. “Yo no quiero llegar a eso porque conllevaría que tenemos un problema de seguridad máximo”, ha afirmado al ser preguntado por la posibilidad de que España vuelva a implantar la mili, una medida que algunos países europeos han puesto sobre la mesa ante el deterioro de la situación internacional. Durante su intervención, Feijóo ha defendido que el debate sobre el gasto militar no debe abordarse “con tanta frivolidad y tanto populismo”. Para justificar su postura, ha puesto como ejemplo a Polonia, cuya frontera con Rusia atraviesa, según ha señalado, un momento de enorme tensión. “Cuando está en riesgo la integridad de tu país, cuando está en riesgo tu propia vida, cuando está en riesgo tu sistema de libertades, ¿qué has de hacer? ¿Has de dejar que te invadan?”, ha planteado el dirigente popular. El líder del PP considera que Europa se enfrenta a amenazas en sus dos flancos principales. Por un lado, ha situado a Rusia y la invasión de Ucrania como el principal problema de la frontera oriental. Por otro lado, ha advertido del riesgo potencial que, a su juicio, representa la frontera sur. “La frontera este, el problema es Putin. La frontera sur tiene un problema humanitario de enorme envergadura”, ha afirmado. En este sentido, ha reclamado que España refuerce sus alianzas con los socios europeos y con la OTAN para garantizar su seguridad y proteger su convivencia. Feijóo ha insistido en que la defensa de la integridad territorial y de las libertades debe ocupar un lugar prioritario en el debate político y ha pedido evitar la demagogia en una cuestión que considera fundamental para el futuro de Europa.

articles.summary: Sen. Bernie Sanders is backing Sen. Chris Van Hollen for the role of Senate Democratic leader, as Van Hollen challenges Sen. Chuck Schumer for the role.
articles.body: Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., is backing Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., for the role of Senate Democratic leader. "The American people voted for change. They want a Democratic Party that will stand up to powerful special interests, take on the billionaire class and fight for working families. That is why I am supporting Senator Chris Van Hollen to lead Senate Democrats," Sanders said in a Thursday post on X. Van Hollen threw his hat into the ring for the role on Thursday, mounting a challenge against current Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., who is looking to retain the Senate Democratic leader position to serve as Senate majority leader next year. "In this election, Americans called on us to unrig an economy rigged against working people & fueled by political corruption. To deliver, we need new leadership. This isn't about any one person – it’s about answering that call. That's why I’m running for Senate Majority Leader," Van Hollen said in a Thursday post on X. I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together—55 seats and counting is an amazing result—and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader. I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people." Sanders had said during a Tuesday press conference that he would not support Schumer for re-election as Senate Democratic leader. During an interview on an episode of "The Weekly Show with Jon Stewart," Sanders said that he would support Van Hollen if he decided to run for the role. Which is why I’m proud to stand with him in his bid to lead our Senate majority," El-Sayed wrote in a Thursday post on X when sharing Van Hollen's announcement. articles.title: Jordi Wild le pregunta a Pedro Sánchez por los cánticos contra él: "De repente ha empezado con el Pedro Sánchez hijo de p***"
articles.standfirst: La del presidente del Gobierno era una de las entrevistas más esperadas en 'The Wild Project'
articles.summary: La del presidente del Gobierno era una de las entrevistas más esperadas en 'The Wild Project'
articles.body: El presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, y candidato del PSOE a las elecciones generales del 29 de noviembre ha pasado por 'The Wild Project'. El conductor del pódcast, Jordi Wild, ha planteado una extensa entrevista, emitida este viernes, con el dirigente socialista. Al inicio de la conversación, el youtuber le ha preguntado por los cánticos contra su persona. "Incluso se han dado en eventos míos y te juro que yo no escuché eso. Escuché quiero sangre, pero luego me di cuenta...", ha explicado. Pedro Sánchez no ha dudado en responder: "Te agradezco el posicionamiento que tuviste. Lo siento más en algunas experiencias que han vivido mis hijas donde de repente el pincha ha empezado con el 'Pedro Sánchez hijo de puta'. Y mis hijas han tenido que salir del local". El presidente del Gobierno ha lamentado que esto se haya convertido, como ha comentado Jordi Wild, en un meme. "Yo no creo que sea un meme porque el meme al final lo hace alguien. Lo comparo mucho con la motosierra de Milei. La gente ve la motosierra, pero se queda con el ruido. El mensaje es la motosierra. Son los recortes, es la austeridad, el sacrificar políticas públicas para la protección del más débil", ha comentado. El candidato del PSOE ha reflexionado en lo que implica este insulto: "En el caso del Pedro Sánchez hijo de puta, para mí lo que hay detrás de ese insulto lo que hay detrás es una carencia total de argumentos y de proyecto político. Que lo haga un chaval pues no es que esté justificado, pero lo que me parece injustificable es que lo diga un responsable político". "Mis abuelos no sabían leer ni escribir y eso me abrió una herida de compromiso con la justicia social. Estamos pasando tantas cosas, Inteligencia Artificial, cambio climático, ascenso de la ultraderecha... Para alguien que ama la política es momento de dar un paso al frente y no un paso al lado", ha reflexionado Pedro Sánchez durante la entrevista. "Yo amo mi oficio y hay cosas más positivas que negativas. Lo positivo es la posibilidad de cambiar cosas, de hacer. Con todos los defectos que he podido cometer, creo que hoy vive uno de sus mejores momentos de la historia democrática", ha insistido. Pedro Sánchez fue el último de los líderes políticos invitados por Jordi Wild en aceptar la invitación. La entrevista al presidente en 'The Wild Project' era una de las más esperadas. El PSOE, así como el resto de las formaciones políticas, han visto la oportunidad de acercarse a nuevos públicos a través de un canal de YouTube con 7,4 millones de seguidores.

articles.title: Alaskans vote to keep ranked choice voting, open primaries
articles.summary: Alaskans have rejected another effort to repeal the Last Frontier’s ranked choice voting system and open primaries, Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) projects. Alaska adopted ranked choice voting and open primaries in a 2020 ballot measure, first implementing the system in the 2022 election cycle along with new campaign finance rules. But opponents haven’t let up…
articles.body:
Alaskans have rejected another effort to repeal the Last Frontier’s ranked choice voting system and open primaries, Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) projects.

Alaska adopted ranked choice voting and open primaries in a 2020 ballot measure, first implementing the system in the 2022 election cycle along with new campaign finance rules. But opponents haven’t let up on efforts to undo the changes.

In 2024, a proposed repeal was narrowly rejected by less than 1 percentage point. This year’s similar measure was backed by top Republicans, as Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy, Rep. Nick Begich (Alaska) and President Trump called for its end .

Only Alaska and Maine use ranked choice voting statewide. Under the system, voters rank candidates in order of preference. If no candidate gets more than 50 percent of first-choice votes in the first round of counting, the candidate with the fewest votes gets eliminated and their support is redistributed to those voters’ second preference.

Alaska also uses open, top-four primaries, in which all candidates appear on the same primary ballot regardless of party. The four highest-scoring contenders advance to the general election.

Supporters say the system helps eliminate vote-splitting and potential spoiler candidates .

Opponents of the system, many of whom have been Republican leaders in the state, have argued it’s too confusing for voters.

In the 2022 special election for the House, for example, a fifth of Begich’s voters did not make a second-choice pick as he lost to Democrat Mary Peltola.

The “no” vote on this year’s Ballot Measure 2 keeps in place the open primary system and ranked choice voting in the general election, rejecting a proposed reversal to party primaries. It also holds onto the campaign finance provisions established in the 2020 ballot measure.

articles.title: A seven-decade presidential election trend predicts Democrats will win in 2028
articles.summary: Based on the historical pattern of the open-seat phenomenon where the incumbent’s party loses seven of eight such races since World War II, current trends suggest a Democrat will win the 2028 presidential election unless specific economic and approval conditions are met.
articles.body:
A strong historical trend in presidential elections suggests that Democrats will win the White House in 2028. Let’s call it the “open seat phenomenon.” An open seat occurs when an incumbent president does not seek another term, either by law or by choice.

Since World War II, there have been eight open-seat presidential elections. The incumbent president’s party has lost seven of them. Only the Republican victory in 1988 interrupted the trend.

Can those winning circumstances from 40 years ago apply to the Republicans in their 2028 open-seat race?

In 1952, the White House shifted from Democrat to Republican. This came after President Harry S. Truman announced that he would not seek a full second term. The previous month, his job approval rating had fallen to 22 percent. He had already served nearly eight years, beginning on April 12, 1945, after President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s death. Truman governed through many of the 20th century’s most tumultuous years. But then Republicans won in a landslide , electing World War II hero General Dwight D. Eisenhower.

In 1960, the presidency went back to the Democrats. After Eisenhower’s two terms, Sen. John F. Kennedy (D-Mass.) defeated incumbent Vice President Richard Nixon (R). At 43, Kennedy embodied youthful optimism, a commitment to national service, and leadership for the new decade.

Then, in 1968, Kennedy’s successor President Lyndon Johnson declined to run a second full term amid growing unpopularity over the raging Vietnam War. Consequently, former Vice President Richard Nixon defeated Johnson’s Vice President, Hubert Humphrey (D).

The exceptional year was 1988. After two landslide victories in 1980 and 1984, President Ronald Reagan’s job approval averaged 53 percent in the months before Election Day. His popularity, coupled with a robust economy, propelled Vice President George H.W. Bush to win Reagan’s “third term” with 53 percent of the vote. Bush won the Electoral College with 426 votes — the last president to receive more than 400.

The next open presidential election took place in 2000. President Bill Clinton (D) was term-limited and remained popular despite having been impeached in 1998. Nonetheless, his vice president, Al Gore (D), lost to Texas Gov. George W. Bush (R) in a controversial election in which Gore won the national popular vote. After a five-to-four Supreme Court decision , the Florida recount was halted. Bush won Florida by only 537 votes and was awarded the state’s 25 Electoral College votes, bringing his total to 271 — just enough for the presidency.

In 2008, the younger President Bush was quite unpopular , as the “Great Recession” had begun and the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan were continuing. The Republican nominee, Sen. John McCain (R-Ariz.), was no match for Illinois Sen. Barack Obama, who promised “hope and change.” Obama won decisively , ending the Bush era and celebrated as the nation’s first African American president.

Then in 2016, after President Obama’s two terms, Republicans won with President Trump , a celebrity businessman with no political experience. In a shocking upset, Trump defeated Hillary Clinton (D), a former U.S. senator, first lady, and secretary of State. Although Trump won the Electoral College, Clinton won the popular vote.

Then, in 2024, incumbent President Joe Biden appeared on track to lose reelection. Democratic leaders all but forced him to withdraw just 107 days before Election Day, triggering an open-seat” election. Vice President Kamala Harris (D) was quickly nominated , but Trump defeated her, capitalizing on the nation’s dour mood and Biden’s unpopularity. Trump’s victory marked a historic comeback after his 2020 loss.

So what about 2028? The incumbent president’s party has lost seven of the eight open-seat presidential elections over seven decades. So what caused Reagan’s vice president to buck the losing trend in 1988?

If Republicans are to win Trump’s “third term,” they must satisfy two criteria and receive a gift from Democrats.

First, Trump must boost his job approval rating above 50 percent. It is currently in the dumps at 38 percent on average.

Second, Bush ran on continuing Reagan’s successful economic policies. In 1988, GDP growth was nearly 4.2 percent. By comparison, 2026 GDP growth is a paltry 1.7 percent , down from 2025.

Most importantly, Trump will have to resolve the affordability crisis, partially tied to his own tariffs and the unpopular Iran war . Only then will voters support a Republican nominee who pledges to continue the president’s policies.

If not, 2028 hopefuls — some quietly, some openly — will distance themselves from Trump. They will seek to forge a new Republican era as a chaotic rebirth sparks intra-party warfare and angers the mercurial incumbent.

But don’t discount Democrats gifting Republicans a weak, out-of-touch liberal nominee. That was key to 1988, when they nominated Massachusetts Gov. Mike Dukakis (D). Even so, Republicans will face a tough election cycle and probably lose, unless Trump’s job approval and economic conditions improve significantly.

Myra Adams served on the creative team of two Republican presidential campaigns in 2004 and 2008. Read more from her archive at The Hill .

articles.title: Jeffries shredded over Hegseth impeachment snafu as Dem jockeys for speaker’s gavel
articles.summary: Eleven absent House Democrats handed Republicans a win on the Pete Hegseth impeachment vote, raising questions about Hakeem Jeffries' leadership.
articles.body: Back-to-back blunders on the House floor are raising questions over whether Democrats are ready for primetime as they're poised to take over the majority — and Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., makes a bid for the top role. Democrats are projected to win 255 House seats, with 12 races yet to be called, and Jeffries is running to be Speaker of the House following the sweeping victories last week that saw the party make gains even in traditional Republican strongholds like Texas, Mississippi, Kansas and South Carolina. But some have questioned whether the recent snafus signal that Jeffries and other leaders may not be ready to be in command of the House majority. "I may have to rethink my support of Hakeem Jeffries after the Hegseth impeachment vote," Fred Trump III, a Democrat, author and nephew of President Donald Trump, posted on X. "Eleven Democrats do not show up? All Republicans vote it down." "Pete Hegseth is laughing at you and is stronger today. Shame," he continued. "A slap in the face of the military and veterans on this important day." HEGSETH THWARTS GOP-LED IMPEACHMENT PUSH AS QUESTIONS SWIRL OVER WHETHER ALLEGATIONS RISE TO HIGH CRIMES House GOP leaders successfully blocked Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., from leading the charge to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth earlier this week. Part of the reason for the failure was the absence of 11 House Democrats during a procedural vote on Tuesday evening. Had just seven of them been present, the vote to kill Massie's impeachment resolution would have failed, triggering debate and a vote on impeaching the Cabinet secretary likely the next day. "Everyone knew that attendance was key tonight but somehow Democratic leaders failed to deliver and handed Republicans a win," Demand Progress Executive Director Sean Vitka said in a statement. 'THE VIEW' CO-HOST CALLS DEMOCRATS MISSING HEGSETH IMPEACHMENT VOTE A 'SELF-INFLICTED WOUND' Progressive journalist David Schuster wrote on X, "Sure, house Dems will have 259 seats in January instead of current 213. And Hegseth impeachment can be reintroduced. But Hakeem having 11 Dem absences today on Hegseth (thus losing vote) reveals a Hakeem leadership problem. Embarrassing." An emotional Rep. Melanie Stansbury, D-N.M., said in a video posted to X that she and other Democrats were stuck in traffic when they missed the vote. Various reports, however, said they were at a fundraiser less than two miles from the U.S. Capitol. HOUSE DEM MISSES HEGSETH IMPEACHMENT VOTE BECAUSE OF MAJOR MEDICAL PROCEDURE ONE WEEK AFTER ELECTION DAY Others blamed medical procedures and family emergencies. The day after, a bill Democratic leadership was actively urging lawmakers to vote against passed by unanimous voice vote — simply because no Democrats called for a roll call instead. Democrats accused Republicans of parliamentary tricks, including a post on the X account belonging to the House Veterans Affairs Committee minority, "Republicans pushed it through that way intentionally so their members wouldn’t have to go on the record supporting cuts to veterans’ benefits." But the majority of Democrats do not believe it is an early blight on Jeffries' potential speakership. HAKEEM JEFFRIES DECLARES BID FOR HOUSE SPEAKER AFTER GOP'S MIDTERM MASSACRE "I think there's frustration in terms of whipping votes. I'm not entirely sure where the breakdown is. And it does seem like there's maybe some tension somewhere," Democratic strategist Mike Nellis told Fox News Digital. "I think it'll be incumbent on the incoming speaker to make sure that everybody feels like they're on the same page ... beyond that, if you're asking me if it makes a difference in a leadership flight, I mean, nobody's running against Hakeem. I haven't heard of anybody seriously thinking about doing that, so I don't know that it'll change anything." He said House Democrats largely "have faith" in Jeffries and House Minority Whip Katherine Clark, D-Mass., who is poised to be the next House Majority Leader. Democrat Dan Turrentine, co-host of "The Huddle," told Fox News Digital "a few Democrats unintentionally missed one vote. Unfortunately, this happens periodically in both chambers, for both parties. It does not speak to Jeffries' leadership." And other House Democrats, when asked, directed frustration at their colleagues instead. "My message is always to members that we need to be here and be on time," Clark told reporters Wednesday. "But there was a clear message from the Republican Party as well that they are unwilling, even after this election, to stand up against Hegseth in this war." Rep. Jared Moskowitz, D-Fla., said, "It's unfortunate, but that's not on leadership." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital reached out to Jeffries' political team for comment.

articles.title: How the Alaska Senate vote count could play out from here
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ The last uncalled Senate race ▪ Huang to testify before Congress ▪ Zelensky says Starshield slowed again ▪ Trump threatens Mexico over caravan Alaska will release another batch of votes tonight that could show whether Democrat Mary Peltola is on track to win the country’s last uncalled Senate race outright or…
articles.body:
Alaska will release another batch of votes tonight that could show whether Democrat Mary Peltola is on track to win the country’s last uncalled Senate race outright or whether it will come down to ranked choice voting.

Peltola leads Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan by nearly 6,000 votes, according to Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). She has 48.92 percent of first-choice votes and needs to finish above 50 percent to win outright.

DDHQ estimates that about 55,000 votes still need to be counted, while The Associated Press puts that number closer to 40,000. Tonight’s vote update is expected to account for much of the remaining vote, though the size of the batch is unclear.

The tranche of ballots could boost Peltola — with roughly 16,500 expected from Anchorage, where Peltola has led so far, and about 9,000 expected from Southeast Alaska, where results have been more mixed but have still favored Peltola.

The outstanding ballots also include absentee ballots, which have so far favored Peltola. Today is the deadline for domestic mail ballots to arrive, while overseas ballots can arrive through Wednesday.

“There still is a path for Senator Sullivan to win, but, at the moment, Mary Peltola appears to be the favorite in this race,” said Russell Luke , a political scientist at the University of Alaska Fairbanks.

Here are some ways the race could play out from here.

If tonight’s update adds about 30,000 votes in the Senate race, Peltola would need to win roughly 62 percent of them to cross the 50 percent threshold. And she would need to maintain that margin until all first-choice votes are counted Wednesday to win outright.

Whether the race is called tonight depends on how far Peltola gets above the 50 percent threshold and how many ballots are still outstanding. If she hovers just over 50 percent with thousands of ballots left to count, the race could remain uncalled until Wednesday.

Luke said a race call tonight for Peltola is “within reach,” but said it’s also likely that Peltola continues gaining ground tonight but still falls short of 50 percent.

“I think that’s entirely possible, though I don’t view it as tremendously likely,” he said about a race call tonight.

Peltola could maintain or even grow her lead but still be short of a majority. If no candidate clears 50 percent once the first-choice count is complete Wednesday, the process moves to ranked choice voting.

Election officials tabulate voters’ rankings by eliminating the lowest-place finisher in each round. Those ballots then transfer to the next candidate that each voter ranked who’s still in the race. Republican Gerald Heikes is in third place with about 5,500 votes, followed by Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. , allegedly recruited by Peltola’s campaign, in fourth place with 4,200.

In FairVote’s analysis of preliminary ballot data, 43 percent of voters who ranked Heikes first preferred the incumbent senator in the final round, compared with 17 percent for Peltola. Those results are switched for voters who ranked the second Sullivan first — 34 percent of those votes go to Peltola in the final round and 23 percent go to the Republican senator. About 4 in 10 ballots in each group would drop out at that point because they didn’t rank any remaining candidates.

In this scenario, Sen. Dan Sullivan gained more from Heikes voters than Peltola gained from the second Sullivan’s voters. Still, a separate Alaska News simulation using Wednesday’s ballot-level data indicated Peltola would be ahead in the final round by roughly 3,000 votes. That would give her the edge in the race, even if she does not win outright.

Sen. Dan Sullivan wins after ranked choice voting

Ranked choice voting is Sen. Dan Sullivan’s only realistic path to victory, Luke said. If tonight’s batch cuts into Peltola’s lead, the incumbent senator would have less ground to make up through transfer votes. He gained ground Wednesday when the state counted a batch of votes predominantly from the Republican-leaning Mat-Su area.

Sullivan could also gain more from transfers if the remaining ballots rank him ahead of Peltola at higher rates than the preliminary data suggest. Luke said some Heikes supporters may have voted for him alone, in which case their ballots would drop out once he’s eliminated. Among those who ranked another candidate, Luke said the votes could split evenly or break toward the senator.

Luke also raised the possibility that some voters ranked both Sullivans because they were unsure which was the incumbent, though he doubted that would account for enough votes to make a difference and noted that the senator was designated as the incumbent on the ballot. Luke said he expected Peltola to pick up more of the second Sullivan’s voters who ranked another candidate, if it gets that far.

▪ The Hill : Kellyanne Conway on GOP ad spending: ‘We lit billions of dollars on fire.’

Democrats are gathering in Denver for a postelection conference and celebration after last week’s decisive victories. As they plan out how they might handle the upcoming two years, I spoke with the chair of the New Democrat Coalition, Rep. Nikki Budzinski (D-Ill.). She warned against looking too far ahead to the 2028 presidential race.

“I think it would be a distraction for our party to immediately pivot to an election that’s two years away when voters said we are feeling pain, pain in our pocketbooks,” Budzinksi said, adding that healthcare and utility bills should remain a top focus.

“Those are the issues that voters want us to be delivering on. And that’s going to be my focus. That should be all Democrats’ focus after last week’s election,” she said.

This will be part of the balancing act that some Democrats have to walk next year. The last two elections have told us that voters are tired of politics that don’t lead to lower costs.

Burman hosts “The Hill” weeknights, 6 p.m. EST/5 p.m. CST on NewsNation.

An outage is continuing to impact Outlook as Microsoft works to get the service back online. Some have begun to report their service has been restored this morning. The company gave an update early this morning that it was seeing “incremental improvement” but didn’t give a timeline for services getting back to normal.

President Trump said he wants to “get Cuba done” before he leaves office and would consider military force to free the country from its communist government. The president has repeatedly flirted with undertaking some type of operation against the Cuban regime in the aftermath of the removal of Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela.

Democrat Eric Jones has defeated Rep. Mike Thompson (D-Calif.) in an intraparty battle, according to a projection from Decision Desk HQ. That makes Thompson the only incumbent House Democrat to lose reelection in the general election. No Republican has successfully ousted an incumbent Democrat this year. Rep.-elect Paul LePage (Maine) was the only Republican to flip a blue seat.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) speaks during a press conference on Monday, April 13, 2026 to discuss an Iran War Powers Resolution as Operation Epic Fury continues on its’ 44th day. (Greg Nash/The Hill)

BATTLE IS ON : Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) announced he will challenge Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) for the position of majority leader, setting up an ideological battle within the Democratic Caucus.

Van Hollen’s decision, announced late Thursday, comes after days of the senator being in “listening mode” about a possible bid. Progressives and other Schumer skeptics have started to rally around Van Hollen as the next leader for Senate Democrats.

“To deliver, we need new leadership. This isn’t about any one person – it’s about answering that call,” Van Hollen said in a post on the social platform X.

Multiple Democrats have declared their opposition to Schumer remaining the leader or at least withheld their support so far, including Sens. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Elissa Slotkin (Mich.) and Sens.-elect Juliana Stratton (Ill.) Adam Hamilton (Kan.), James Talarico (Texas) and Troy Jackson (Maine).

Schumer, who has led the party in the upper chamber for nearly 10 years, insists he has the votes locked up to be majority leader.

“I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead,” he said in a post on X, responding to Van Hollen’s challenge. “I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together—55 seats and counting is an amazing result—and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader.”

▪ CNN : Leadership showdown could fracture Democratic post-election unity.

▪ The Hill : GOP warns Trump that Pentagon funding push risks shutdown.

GRILLING AHEAD : A top Republican told The Hill that Jensen Huang has agreed to appear before Congress for a closed-door briefing in the aftermath of his resignation from Nvidia over reports that he had multiple extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

Rep. Brian Mast (R-Fla.), the chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said lawmakers are negotiating the timing and other details of the appearance. He said the testimony would likely be under oath, transcribed, video recorded and conducted before multiple committees.

Nvidia, one of the country’s largest companies, announced Thursday morning that Huang would step down immediately and be replaced by Colette Kress , the executive vice president and chief financial officer, as interim CEO.

The company’s stock took a sharp dive following Jensen Huang’s resignation, falling nearly 15 percent before rebounding slightly. The stock ultimately finished a little more than 4 percent down at the end of the day Thursday.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) said in a social media post that his resignation “does not absolve him” or the company and that they owe Congress answers .

CIRCLING BACK : Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said his country’s military units recorded disruptions to the speeds at which it can use the Starshield satellite technology for the second time.

Zelensky said Thursday in a post on the social platform X that restrictions were limiting the speed that Starshield could be used to 100 mph, preventing Ukrainian interceptors from reaching sufficient speeds to take down Russian jet-powered drones.

The Hill’s Laura Kelly reports in an exclusive that Sens. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.) and Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) called on Congress to conduct oversight on the reported disruption.

This marks the second time in the past month that Ukraine has dealt with a slowdown of Starshield, the military version of the satellite internet service Starlink, overseen by Elon Musk ‘s SpaceX. Ukraine has come to rely on both throughout its war with Russia.

The most recent slowdown comes as special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are set to meet with Zelensky following their meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in pursuit of a peace deal.

▪ The Washington Post : Witkoff, Kushner say Europe to join peace talks.

▪ Bloomberg : Ukraine says it hit Russia’s biggest oil refinery in Siberia.

SUSPECT ID’D : The suspected gunman believed to have shot five people , including one fatally, in the Logan Circle neighborhood of Washington, D.C., died on Thursday from self-inflicted gunshot wound.

Police have identified the shooter as 55-year-old Matt Lambert , an emergency room doctor. Officials say Lambert shot and killed one person in a VIDA Fitness gym before shooting four other people in multiple locations outside the gym.

The shooter barricaded himself in his apartment and shot himself as police attempted to negotiate with him. A court filing shows Lambert was in an ongoing dispute with his apartment’s management company and was suing over poor living conditions, including water damage and mold.

Officials said they were looking into the dispute as a possible motive.

▪ FOX5 : What we know about the suspect.

▪ The Associated Press : Hunt for clues in deadly Brooklyn building collapse will take time

The president has no public events scheduled.

The House will convene at 10 a.m. for a pro forma session.

Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) speaks during a Congressional spotlight hearing on Capitol Hill, Tuesday, Sept. 22, 2026, in Washington. (Mark Schiefelbein, Associated Press)

GEARING UP : Democrats are preparing for an intense faceoff with the White House and the Justice Department following the preemptive letters the Trump administration sent lawmakers to push back against their planned investigations.

A letter from the White House warned Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), the incoming chair of the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, that upcoming probes could “ cross the line into blatant criminality.” And a U.S. attorney from Texas, Aaron Reitz , accused Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) of “terrorizing entities” when he contacted those who donated to the president’s ballroom construction and other projects.

Blumenthal is set to chair the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations in the next session of Congress.

Garcia told CNN’s Kaitlan Collins that Congress has to “flex all of its power.” He said Democrats would be ready to turn to the courts.

“When you ask people across the country why they were motivated to vote and to bring change, they said the same two things. It was about affordability, and it was about rooting out government corruption. Well, we have a mandate to take on corruption, and certainly the corruption of the Trump family,” he said.

The Hill’s Rebecca Beitsch reports that both sides are accusing the other of overreaching before a single subpoena has even been issued. She notes that the law is largely on the Democrats’ side, as Congress’s investigatory powers have been upheld by the Supreme Court.

Several Democrats told her that they view the correspondence as a sign that their plans have touched a nerve with Trump.

“It just means that Trump is bothered by this,” said Rep. Stephen Lynch (D-Mass.).

▪ The Hill : Trump adviser moves to strike Qatar payment allegations from record.

▪ The Hill Insider : Democrats face backlash after legislative mishaps.

President Trump speaks in the James Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House on Nov. 9, 2026, in Washington. (Alex Brandon, Associated Press)

TURN BACK : Trump threatened to double tariffs on Mexico if a caravan of more than 1,000 migrants reportedly heading to the U.S. is not stopped.

A source in the Chiapas state government in Mexico estimated to Reuters that about 1,500 people, including many families, left from the city of Tapachula near the border with Guatemala on Tuesday. The outlet reported that many migrants saw new reason for optimism following last week’s midterm election results.

Trump vowed Thursday in a post on Truth Social that the migrants won’t be accepted into the U.S. and called on the Mexican government to stop them. If they aren’t stopped, the president said he would retaliate against Mexico with additional tariffs.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum confirmed at a press conference that a group of people are walking north toward the U.S. She said people in the caravan have been informed how difficult it is to enter the U.S. and that Mexico is looking to return them to their countries of origin.

No migrant caravans have arrived at the U.S. border since Trump returned to office last year, Reuters reported.

The outlet reported that the migrants are hoping to reach Mexico City to receive help from the Mexican government and protection against detainment at the U.S.-Mexico border.

“There will be no leniency!” Trump said in his post, adding that he has informed Mexico, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R), Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa (D), U.S. Border Patrol and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement of his stance.

▪ Reuters : Migrants trek through Mexico, in pictures.

Dear new member: Welcome to Congress. Now you can deliver on affordability , former Reps. Cheri Bustos (D-Ill.) and Joe Crowley (D-N.Y.) write in The Hill.

The fall of the A.I. king , Stephen Witt writes in The New York Times.

Former Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas speaks on Oct. 1, 2024, during a briefing at the White House in Washington. (Mark Schiefelbein, Associated Press)

And finally … 👏👏👏 Congrats to this week’s Morning Report quiz winners ! They were ready to go with these quick impeachment facts. Our apologies if anyone who submitted the correct answers doesn’t see their name included. The Outlook outage impacted The Hill as well as many others , seemingly.

Here’s who went 4/4: Stan Wasser, Rick Schmidtke, Jess Elger, Gail White, Richard Baznik, Anna Bednarczyk, Linda L. Field, Laura Rettaliata, Ned Sauthoff, William Chittam, Jenessa Wagner, Mark Ryan, Steve Comer, Harry Strulovici, M. Whitehouse, David P. Bader and Robert Bradley .

Former Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas became just the second-ever Cabinet official to be impeached in 2024. The Senate voted to dismiss the charges without trial. The only other Cabinet member to be impeached was former Secretary of War William Belknap.

Former Vice President John C. Calhoun requested and received an impeachment inquiry into his own conduct when he was accused of bribery, and he was quickly cleared of wrongdoing. Spiro Agnew pointed to that precedent in requesting an inquiry into his own conduct when he faced bribery allegations, but the request was denied as Congress was focused on investigating Richard Nixon’s conduct. Agnew ultimately resigned.

Former Attorney General Harry Daugherty avoided a push for his impeachment during Warren Harding’s administration, but he later resigned at Calvin Coolidge’s request as he was implicated in the Teapot Dome scandal.

Abuse of power is the one not specifically listed as a reason for impeachment, though it was introduced against Nixon, who resigned before he could be impeached, and Trump. The Constitution authorizes impeachment in cases of treason, bribery and “other high crimes and misdemeanors.”

articles.title: ¿Quién ha estado mejor en las entrevistas con Jordi Wild? Encuesta sobre Pedro Sánchez, Feijóo y Ada Colau
articles.standfirst: El youtuber publica sus conversaciones con tres candidatos a presidente
articles.summary: El youtuber publica sus conversaciones con tres candidatos a presidente
articles.body: Jordi Wild ha publicado este viernes 13 de octubre las extensas entrevistas con tres candidatos a presidente del Gobierno. Ada Colau, de Frente Amplio, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, del Partido Popular, y Pedro Sánchez, del PSOE, han pasado por 'The Wild Project'. Las entrevistas se han publicado de forma prácticamente simultánea. El conductor del pódcast ha sido fiel a sus promesas y ha firmado entrevistas serias y extensas, esto último siempre habitual en su formato, que han contado además con la presencia de verificadores. Los tres partidos políticos han visto en la invitación de Jordi Wild una oportunidad para acercarse a un público distinto, más joven, de cara a las elecciones generales del próximo 29 de noviembre. Rodeados de pósters de películas, anime y videojuegos, un escenario que se aleja del clásico plató de televisión, los tres candidatos han dejado titulares interesantes y han abordado numerosas cuestiones de actualidad. Las entrevistas ya están publicadas en el canal de YouTube de Jordi Wild, con 7,4 millones de seguidores en la plataforma, después de la gran expectación de los últimos días. Los analistas políticos debaten ahora sobre quién de los tres ha salido más o menos reforzado del paso por un formato al que no están habituados de cara a los comicios generales. ¿Quién cree que ha sacado más rendimiento de su paso por 'The Wild Project'? ¿Qué candidato o candidata le ha sorprendido más? Santiago Abascal ha sido el gran ausente en la serie de entrevistas en 'The Wild Project'. El candidato de VOX se comprometió a acudir al pódcast, pero tras su paso por 'La Revuelta', presentado por David Broncano, su formación cambió de opinión. Esta decisión ha generado una gran polémica en los últimos días y ha provocado el enfado de Jordi Wild. El catalán ha reconocido que no esperaba este giro de timón del partido de Abascal.

articles.title: Opinion - Don’t be fooled: There is nothing moderate about the new Democratic Congress
articles.summary: Brace yourselves, America: This is not your grandparents’ Democratic Party.
articles.body:
Brace yourselves, America: This is not your grandparents' Democratic Party.

It isn't the party of John F. Kennedy or Bill Clinton or the late Sen. Bill Proxmire (D-Wis.), who used to poke fun at ridiculous government waste . JFK, after all, pushed through tax cuts , and Clinton oversaw bipartisan welfare reform . This new crop of Democrats have never met a spending bill they didn't like or a bloated fraud-riddled entitlement program they don't support.

It is a radical new group that has taken over the U.S. Congress , led by people who hate successful businesses, want to confiscate your wealth, see corruption in prosperity (but not in big government) and have no clue what has historically made our nation thrive.

The liberal media is working overtime to convince us otherwise. A headline from The Economist blares : "The blue wave was powered by moderate Democrats." Third Way claims : "Moderates Made Democratic Majorities." And The New York Times highlighted : "Moderate Democrats increased their numbers," explaining that "Their victories in competitive or Republican-leaning states and districts have fundamentally altered the balance of power among Democrats in Congress."

But just because a bunch of Democrats were elected to seats in red or purple states, it does not mean that they are moderates.

Take Annie Andrews , who beat Darline Graham to win a Senate seat in deep-red South Carolina. Andrews is a doctor who in the past has supported giving minors irreversibly life-altering puberty blockers and other treatments to assist with their gender transitions — a practice disapproved of by all sane adults. Is she a "moderate"?

Or how about Josh Turek , the new senator from red-state Iowa, who supports eliminating right-to-work laws and wants to jack up the federal minimum wage? Or Abdul El-Sayed, the Medicare-for-all enthusiast elected to represent Michigan in the Senate?

Consider who is now ascending to positions of power.

Come January, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) will head the U.S. Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs . Warren is a die-hard progressive who hates the banks she is about to oversee. Why? Because her father, whom she calls "daddy" in her memoir, "A Fighting Chance," couldn't hold a job and almost caused the family to lose their home to a supposedly heartless bank. In a heart-rending scene, her mother is forced to go to work in order to pay the mortgage. It was clearly a defining moment for Warren.

On the campaign trail, she describes "Big Tech CEOs, Wall Street executives, and giant corporations" as "ripping off the American people to make themselves richer." She accused oil companies of price-gouging when prices went up, then claimed the cost of Thanksgiving turkeys rose (when Joe Biden was in the White House) due to "plain old corporate greed."

As head of one of the Senate's most powerful committees, Warren will push to cap interest rates on credit cards, investigate the biggest banks and pass her "Stop Wall Street Looting Act," which would exert numerous requirements on private equity firms, which she dubs "legal looters." She will try to block mergers, accusing them generally of creating monopoly powers, and break up existing combinations like those linking insurance companies and pharmacies.

In a recent op-ed for Time magazine, Warren writes, "Democrats won by being populist economic fighters who were unafraid to call out the corrupt politicians and corporate interests who have rigged the system at the expense of everyone else." That is her mindset.

Partnering with Warren, incredibly, is Rep. Maxine Waters (D-Calif.), considered likely to chair the House Financial Services Committee.

Like her colleagues, Waters promises to root out corruption in the Trump White House. But in 2010, the House Ethics Committee formally charged Waters with three counts of violating House rules regarding conflicts of interest. Anyone who doesn't think that threat will bedevil those party leaders (and others) and guide Democrats' policy going forward is not paying attention.

Liz Peek is a former partner of major bracket Wall Street firm Wertheim and Company.

articles.title: Whole Hog Politics: Will the blue wave wash away the Electoral College?
articles.summary: [Watch Whole Hog Politics Live: Hill Insider members can join us live today at 9 a.m. EST as Chris Stirewalt and host Bill Sammon go deep on this week’s political news. Members can join the discussion and pose their questions to Bill and Chris. Tune in!] It took North Carolina Democrats 16 years to win…
articles.body:
[ Watch Whole Hog Politics Live : Hill Insider members can join us live today at 9 a.m. EST as Chris Stirewalt and host Bill Sammon go deep on this week’s political news. Members can join the discussion and pose their questions to Bill and Chris. Tune in! ]

It took North Carolina Democrats 16 years to win back their state’s House of Representatives, but last week they finally did it.

The Tar Heel State’s lower chamber had been blue for most of the 1990s and the aughts, but in the 2010 red wave, Republicans not only won a decisive majority in the House, but scored their first trifecta — unified partisan control of the House, Senate and governorship — in more than a century.

The state’s Democrats may end up a couple of hundred votes short in a single state Senate race from having a new trifecta of their own, but the wipeout of the GOP in North Carolina still makes clear the size of the wave that hit Republicans. The congressional delegation appears to be going from 10 Republicans and four Democrats to, once all the votes are counted, 11 Democrats and three Republicans.

Now, there will be those who say that North Carolina’s statehouse Republicans did this to themselves by passing a gerrymandered map in a bid to nick another congressional seat for their party as part of President Trump ’s 2025 redistricting blitz. While it certainly helped mobilize Democrats, it wasn’t exactly a dummymander. There’s no map state Republicans could have drawn that would have survived the 20-point thrashing that Sen.-elect Roy Cooper (D-N.C.) laid on his Republican opponent. Pointless and ultimately self-defeating? Sure. A dummymander? Nah.

The question before Republicans in North Carolina and in many other states is the following: Will it take them as long to claw back control as it did for Democrats in the aftermath of the 2010 trouncing they took? Will it be 2042 (!) before the red wave washes them back out again?

In total, the blue team managed to reclaim 12 state legislative chambers while shattering GOP supermajorities in 13 others. Add five governorships to their tally — with a sixth potentially on the horizon in Alaska — and six new state trifectas in Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, where Democrats now hold both the executive mansion and legislative majorities.

As Democrats enjoy pointing out, with Texas turning blue at the state level, something like three-quarters of all Americans will live in a state with a Democratic governor and more than half will live in a state with a Democratic trifecta. Maybe even of more significance, though, is the fact that for the first time since 2019, the majority of state attorneys general will be Democrats. While governors set a lot of policies, attorneys general have been the shock troops of the legal fights between state and federal policies.

But the most consequential change from all that bluing of the statehouses could be in how America conducts its presidential elections.

Nevada’s Democratic governor-elect is already on board for adding the state to the National Popular Vote Compact, and lawmakers in many other states are lining up to join the pact to realize the long-sought progressive goal of circumventing the Electoral College.

The compact was born after former President George W. Bush ’s 2000 Electoral College victory and reinvigorated following Trump’s win in 2016. The District of Columbia and 18 states — starting with Maryland in 2007 and continuing through Virginia this year — have joined the effort. That puts 222 electoral votes in their column, just 48 shy of the 270-vote threshold they need to enact the plan.

As states initially signed up, the possibility of actually hacking the Constitution seemed unlikely. It was a way for Democratic lawmakers to lodge their protest against the Bush and Trump victories, but with the safety of knowing that it wouldn’t actually happen until there were states with an outright electoral majority which, until last week, seemed like a remote possibility. Now, a low-risk bet is suddenly a high-stakes proposition.

Now, this might seem a crazy choice for a party that lost the national popular vote in the most recent presidential election, but we should remember that one of the defining traits of 21st century American politics is that neither party believes that the other side’s majorities are legitimate. Both Democrats and Republicans believe that were it left to the voluntatem populi without the interference of the dirty tricks of their opponents, their side would always prevail. Plus, populism and progressivism generally hold that more direct democracy is a good thing.

I will not bore you here with all the detailed reasons why a national popular vote is a catastrophically bad idea but will instead list the two most pungent: First, it creates bad incentives for election fraud and makes resolving disputed outcomes even harder. Having just one number to challenge or rig invites much worse depredations than the effort to overturn the 2020 election gave us. Second, it breeds more populism and more angry-mob politics. If you haven’t enjoyed Trumpism and the idea of $5,000 bonus checks, you would most certainly not enjoy the America of a national popular vote. Democrats should bear in mind that much of the world — including our own country — has shown in the past 20 years that right-wing populism often beats the left-wing version.

What remains to be seen, though, is whether the compact would actually hold if progressives succeed in the coming two years.

Not only would the effort face constitutional challenges if it was actually invoked — the idea that a state can really bind its presidential electors to the outcomes of other states’ elections is an open question — there’s the possibility of noncompliance. If a Republican wins the national popular vote, will a Democratic state call an emergency session and repeal the law before the votes can be certified?

Maybe, like the Equal Rights Amendment and the Balanced Budget Amendment, the National Popular Vote Compact will moulder in legislative twilight indefinitely, or maybe we are getting ready to kick off one of the biggest donnybrooks in an era already defined by an ongoing constitutional stress test.
