As the planet cools, ocean water becomes locked up in continental ice sheets, and sea levels fall by hundreds of feet. Eventually the planet starts warming again, the ice melts, and sea levels rise once more. During the past million years or so, this cycle has repeated itself many times. … If you were able to speed up the glacial cycle and watch it from space, you’d observe the ebb and flow of a planetary tide—one that over the course of millennia alternately exposes and submerges immense expanses of land along the continental shelves. The result, as … [ Jerome E. Dobson , a professor emeritus of geography at the University of Kansas] writes, is ‘a vast earth feature,’ bounded by the highest and lowest sea levels of the glacial cycle, that ‘transforms back and forth among upland, wetland, and seafloor.’”

Vance wants a crowded field: Politico : “[ Vice President Vance ] sees an opening in the post-election blame game: Republican hawks are attacking him for opposing the war, Democrats promise retribution — and he’s planning to use both to prove he’s the anti-establishment voice in Washington. … ‘Those swings from JD’s critics are doing the job for him,’ a person close to Vance told Playbook. ‘Unpopular DC insiders criticizing him for not being a sufficient enough war hawk is not necessarily a bad thing for him politically and sends the right signal to our base,’ the person said. ‘These people are doing the lord’s work as far as I’m concerned.’ … An embattled Vance will encourage other Republicans to join the field, and play into his strategy for 2028, the person told Playbook. ‘We want as many people to jump in to divide up the anti-JD vote,’ the person said. ‘The worst thing would be a two or three-way. It would be much more of a fight.’”

But Trump nixes veep’s role as peacemaker: The Wall Street Journal : “President Trump said Thursday that the U.S. didn’t need a deal with Iran and would prefer Vice President JD Vance, who has taken the lead in negotiations, work on investigating American cities run by Democrats. ‘I have asked Vice President Vance to focus his complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S.,’ Trump posted on social media. ‘We don’t need a deal with Iran.’ … The move comes as Vance had opened a communications channel with Mohsen Rezaei , the hard-line secretary of Iran’s top security body, and considered face-to-face talks with him. … Trump’s move is a sudden reversal. In recent days, the president had told top aides and counterparts that he was open to Vance restarting talks with Iran and had empowered him to negotiate.”

And then there’s the whole curse thing: Silver Bulletin : “Which other vice presidents sought the presidency after serving under presidents who were unpopular near the end of their presidencies? Bush, Biden and Gore don’t count because Reagan, Obama and Clinton were reasonably popular as of the end of their terms. Humphrey lost. Ford lost. Mondale lost in a landslide. Quayle and Pence had no hope of winning their nominations. Harris lost, narrowly. Among the VPs to relatively popular presidents, Gore lost too. Biden won after a four-year hiatus but is likely to be remembered by history as having held on too long in seeking a second term. H.W. Bush is the clearest success story but, like Biden, was a one-termer. Sure, a couple of those elections — Gore’s certainly — might have gone the other way. But in recent years, we’ve added Harris and Pence as failures.”

Ocasio-Cortez grassroots group gears up: The Hill : “Progressives are gearing up for the 2028 election cycle with the launch of a new group meant to draw Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) into the presidential race. Ready for AOC launched Monday aiming to demonstrate support for the popular legislator as speculation about a White House run mounts. Supporters are asked to sign a pledge to vote for Ocasio-Cortez for president, to volunteer for her campaign and to spread the word about why they want the New York Democrat to run. … The democratic socialist has publicly mulled a presidential bid, as the far-left flank has notched a number of high-profile election wins across the country. She told The New York Times in September that she would make a decision after the midterm elections, adding that ‘sometimes life just makes things ready for you.’”

As she makes big moves with her team: Axios : “New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is shaking up her team for the second time in the past few months as she prepares to make the biggest decision of her political life. The overhaul comes as the democratic socialist leader is debating whether to run for president in 2028 — or Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer ‘s seat, which is up the same year. Ocasio-Cortez has parted ways with her longtime digital fundraising firm, Middle Seat, according to three people familiar with the decision. At the same time, sources said, she’s brought on Aisle 518 Strategies — the company led by Democratic strategist Tim Tagaris , who oversaw Bernie Sanders ’ record-breaking online fundraising strategy in his two presidential campaigns.”

Will she or won’t she? Harris at the crossroads: The Washington Sun: “[Former Vice President] Kamala Harris has a decision to make — and the clock is ticking on when those close to her say she should make up her mind. Advisers and friends in Harris’ orbit have told the former vice president that she should decide by the end of this year whether to make another run at the White House, according to three sources familiar with the conversation, arguing that drawing it out much beyond that would be unfair to the nearly two-dozen candidates expected to run. The sources said that while Harris heard their arguments, she hasn’t agreed to any decision deadline. ‘I won’t set a timeline for this, but my decision will largely depend on my family,’ the former vice president told Swiss newspaper Tages-Anzeiger during a post-midterms trip. Those close to her say she’s conflicted about launching another presidential bid — which would be her second primary run and third bid overall after replacing then-President Joe Biden on the 2024 ticket.”

articles.body: Secretary of State Marco Rubio will deliver his first major speech apart from his diplomatic duties Friday following the GOP’s blowout midterm losses, with some attendees at the Federalist Society's National Lawyers Convention eager to hear how he will chart a path forward as the 2028 presidential race draws closer. I hope he addresses the foreign policy implications and how he thinks foreign policy played a role into that, into the election results." Rubio will deliver an approximately 45-minute speech for the Barbara Olson Memorial Lecture, whose previous speakers include former Attorney General Bill Barr and The Free Press founder Bari Weiss. But another question weighs heavily on the minds of attendees at the annual conference in Washington, D.C., which attracts prominent lawyers affiliated with the conservative movement. HOUSE CONSERVATIVE EMERGES WITH 2028 PRESIDENTIAL PICK AFTER GOP'S MIDTERM MASSACRE: 'I AM ALL IN' "There are a lot of people in the room who are going to be wondering if he's still planning on running for president someday," Rachel Paulose, a former U.S. attorney and general counsel at Upper Midwest Law Center, told Fox News Digital. "That will be a question that will be top of mind for a lot of people." The question comes following a CNN report citing officials close to Vice President JD Vance — often described as President Donald Trump's MAGA heir apparent — who expressed concern that Republicans would not be able to win the 2028 presidential race if the Iran war remains an issue during the campaign. Republicans lost a net 41 House seats and eight Senate seats, with Alaska's Senate race still undecided, marking the largest simultaneous loss in both chambers of Congress for Republicans in a midterm election since 1958. President Donald Trump has partly blamed the losses on voters' opposition to the Iran war, and Vance was more direct about the war's impact on the election results, though Rubio has yet to weigh in. "The fact of the matter is that the Republicans got blown out pretty well in the recent election," John Shu, a legal commentator who served in the administrations of former Presidents George H. W. Bush and George W. Bush, told Fox News Digital. "And it's possible that he may talk about the budgetary process. It'll be interesting to see what the Democratic House and the Democrat Senate will do regarding funding of the State Department." Shu said Rubio could also address U. S. strikes on suspected drug cartels off the coast of Venezuela in fall 2025, which drew sharp criticism from Democratic lawmakers, including six Democrats with military or intelligence backgrounds who released a video urging service members to disobey unlawful orders. I mean, he's the secretary of state," Shu said. Trump has previously floated a 2028 ticket pairing Vance and Rubio, who at one point held four senior administration roles simultaneously and became the subject of a running internet joke about his expanding portfolio. articles.title: Democrats won — but so did election integrity
articles.summary: Voters demonstrated that supporting Democratic candidates does not require them to oppose voter ID or the integrity of the vote.
articles.body:
Democrats had plenty of reasons to rejoice on Election Night. They won governorships, captured Senate seats, and flipped legislative chambers across the country. But buried beneath the headlines was another election outcome that Washington’s political class would just as soon not acknowledge.

Voter identification and citizenship requirements did well. In fact, in many states, they did substantially better than the Democrats who won the elections.

Voters in eight states approved three ballot initiatives to strengthen voter identification requirements and five measures to explicitly reserve voting for American citizens.

Ohio voters elected Democrat Amy Acton governor and flipped a Republican-held U.S. Senate seat by electing Democrat Sherrod Brown. Yet nearly 3 million Ohioans voted to amend their state constitution to require voter identification. Issue 3 passed with more than 65 percent support, receiving over 530,000 more votes than Acton and over 630,000 more than Brown.

Ohio already had three years of experience with its photo ID requirement. Voters weren’t being asked to trust an unproven experiment — they voted to ensure the protections they had already adopted cannot be erased by the next legislative majority.

In Nevada, Democrats took control of the governor’s mansion, but voters also passed Question 7 . Carrying more than 62 percent of the vote, Question 7 requires photo identification for in-person voting and identity verification for vote-by-mail ballots. Over 100,000 additional Nevadans voted for voter identification over either of the leading Democratic candidates for governor and lieutenant governor.

Perhaps the most telling example of the issue transcending party lines came in North Carolina. Democrats picked up the state House for the first time since 1972 and gained ground in the state Senate. They also sent former Democratic Governor Roy Cooper to the U.S. Senate with nearly 59 percent of the vote. But on the same ballot, nearly 60 percent of North Carolinians voted to strengthen their state constitution’s voter identification protections .

Then there are the states that codified citizenship requirements. At a time when some municipalities have been giving or trying to give noncitizens the vote, voters in Alaska, Arkansas, Kansas, South Dakota, and West Virginia said no, approving measures explicitly reserving American elections for American citizens.

Measure Three carried nearly 70 percent in Alaska . Arkansas Issue One carried nearly 70 percent of the vote — significantly more than the victorious Sen. Tom Cotton (R). In West Virginia, Amendment One received a nearly four-to-one vote. Kansas’ citizenship amendment carried 64 percent and South Dakota’s Amendment J received more than 61 percent .

In Kansas, Democrat Adam Hamilton unseated Sen. Roger Marshall (R), ending a 94-year streak of Republican victories in the state’s U.S. Senate elections. But more than 672,000 Kansans voted for the citizenship amendment — 112,000 votes more than voted for Hamilton.

Oklahoma voters had already approved a constitutional voter identification requirement in August.

Federal law prohibits noncitizens from voting in federal elections. But some jurisdictions allow noncitizens to vote in local elections. Voters in these five states voted to make their own rules clear: State and local elections, like federal elections, are for American citizens.

These results prove that election integrity is an American issue, regardless of which party holds the reins.

Alaska is teaching all of us, in real time, why the rules are so important. Even though Measure Three passed easily, Alaskans still don’t know the outcome of one of the most significant U.S. Senate races in the country. Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) and former Rep. Mary Peltola (D) are locked in a hair’s-breadth race, neither garnering a majority of first-choice votes in the preliminary results.

Because Alaska uses ranked-choice voting, determining the winner may require eliminating candidates and redistributing ballots according to voters’ subsequent rankings. Outstanding eligible ballots must also be counted, and the state won’t perform its ranked-choice tallying until November 18. The fact that two candidates on the ballot share the name Dan Sullivan — apparently due to some dirty tricks — doesn’t help, either.

For years, pundits have tried to turn voter identification and citizenship verification into partisan issues. But voters demonstrated that supporting Democratic candidates does not require them to oppose voter ID or the integrity of the vote.

Political majorities will come and go. But across the nation, voters chose to make basic election protections untouchable by normal political realignments. Washington should take notice. Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) had the SAVE America Act before him and a Republican-majority Senate. He failed to pass it — another Washington failure.

Voters across America just delivered the message that Senate leadership failed to recognize: Election integrity isn’t a political liability. It’s a winning issue, even in states electing Democrats.

Ken Cuccinelli is chairman of Heritage Action’s Election Transparency Initiative and a former acting deputy secretary of Homeland Security and attorney general of Virginia.

articles.summary: President Trump claimed in a new interview that he could “easily” beat former President Obama in a political match-up, days after Republicans experienced sweeping losses in the midterm elections. “I got many more votes than he got, and I got many more votes in the states,” Trump told “Straight Shooter” host Stephen A. Smith in…
articles.body:
President Trump claimed in a new interview that he could “easily” beat former President Obama in a political match-up, days after Republicans experienced sweeping losses in the midterm elections.

“I got many more votes than he got, and I got many more votes in the states,” Trump told “Straight Shooter” host Stephen A. Smith in a sit-down interview at the White House.

“And I have the most of the state records of the big states,” he continued. “If you take a look at Texas, I have the all-time record. Florida, I have the all-time record.”

When pressed by Smith about whether he thought he could “beat Obama,” the president replied, “I think I could beat him easily.”

“I think he’s highly overrated, yeah,” he added.

Trump has repeatedly teased the idea of running for a third term, despite term limits enshrined in the Constitution.

In his interview with Smith, Trump confronted the Republican Party’s defeat in the midterm elections, admitting that GOP voters “didn’t like the candidates” put forward by the party.

However, the president stood by his decision to endorse Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton over Sen. John Cornyn for the GOP nomination in the Texas Senate race, saying the incumbent senator was “very disloyal to me.”

Cornyn “was disloyal at certain parts, when it was perhaps maybe a good thing for him to be, when I wasn’t in as much favor as at other times,” Trump said. “But he wasn’t for me, and I remember that. You know, I have a very good memory.”

Paxton ultimately lost in the general election to Texas state Rep. James Talarico (D), marking a significant victory for the Democratic Party in their fight to flip historically red seats across the country.

The president also defended his administration’s military operations in Iran, which have been met with rising public discontent amid high energy prices tied to the ongoing conflict.

“I think historically that’s going to be a great decision, I hope,” Trump said. “But short-term, I guess, it’s tougher politically. I knew that.”

articles.title: Bessent points finger at Lutnick over Nvidia chip exports as Trump advisers discuss possible Commerce Secretary ouster
articles.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Friday accused the Commerce Department of a delay in labeling Nvidia customer Megaspeed a possible national security threat, publicly airing an ongoing administration blame game following the ouster of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
articles.body: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Friday accused the Commerce Department of a delay in labeling Nvidia customer Megaspeed a possible national security threat, publicly airing an ongoing administration blame game following the ouster of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. His comments come as some of President Donald Trump’s advisers, reeling from the fallout of Huang’s resignation, have begun discussing whether Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick should be dismissed, according to people familiar with the conversations. Trump himself has also fielded calls from administration officials and outside advisors raising alarm bells about Lutnick, two additional people said. So far, the White House has stood by him, issuing a statement Thursday – before Bessent’s comments – saying Trump “maintains complete confidence in the secretary and his ability to carry out the position as the most transformative Commerce Secretary in modern history.” Trump and Lutnick are longtime friends, and sources said it was unclear what the president might do. Speaking on CNBC, Bessent said a wide swath of Trump’s administration — including the Treasury and State departments, the Pentagon and the US Trade Representative — favored placing Megaspeed on an export blacklist. He said it was the Commerce Department, led by Lutnick, that had failed the follow through. “Commerce…has the pen. You would have to ask them about their internal processes,” he said. He suggested the inaction had violated directives given by Trump. “I am frustrated when President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above” a certain technological level, he said. “And so any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts our great companies in the AI race, gives the Chinese an advantage,” he went on. CNN has reached out to the Commerce Department for comment. Trump officials have long harbored concerns that Megaspeed has circumvented US law and funneled advanced chips into China — a prospect that Treasury staffers argued should land it on Commerce’s so-called entity list of China-connected companies that could pose national security risks. But the issue gathered newfound attention and importance in recent days when it was reported publicly that Huang had an affair with a Megaspeed employee suspected of having intelligence connections to China. Senior Trump officials, including Lutnick, were briefed months ago about Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, the Megaspeed executive. Despite those warnings, Commerce has so far refused to put Megaspeed on the entity list, people familiar with the matter said. In a tense Situation Room meeting last week, Bessent challenged Lutnick over his department’s reluctance to blacklist Megaspeed, CNN previously reported. Lutnick did not immediately commit to taking any specific action, they said. In the interview Friday, Bessent did not deny the confrontation. “We don’t repeat conversations in the Situation Room,” he said.

articles.title: Trump says he wants to ‘get Cuba done’ when asked about use of military force
articles.summary: President Donald Trump signaled in a new interview that he could take military action to topple Cuba’s communist government before he leaves office.
articles.body: President Donald Trump signaled in a new interview that he could take military action to topple Cuba’s communist government before he leaves office. “I want to get Cuba done before I leave you,” Trump told conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt on Thursday when asked if he would order the use of military force against Cuba to free the nation. Trump said his administration is “watching it very closely” and Cuba is “doing very poorly,” calling it a “failed” country. The president said he would “certainly consider” taking military action against Cuba. “Frankly, I’d love to be able to do it for the people, for the Cubans that came and were treated really badly, and they came to America,” he said. Speaking about the Cuban government during an impromptu White House news conference Monday, Trump said, “I would imagine it will fall fairly soon.” At a Conservative Political Action Conference event at Mar-a-Lago last week, he said Secretary of State Marco Rubio is “going to work on Cuba” and joked “we’re going to drop him by parachute into Cuba.” Trump made similar comments about Rubio during a campaign rally in Texas in late October, saying, “We’ll drop him in the middle of Cuba. He’ll solve that problem in about two minutes. No, Cuba’s coming our way, just like everything else is coming our way because we are a respected country again.” Days earlier in a post on X, Rubio called on people who “seek to create positive change in Cuba” to “seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete partnership with the CIA.” Trump is still dealing with other conflicts around the world. The president has faced backlash from Democrats and Republicans over the Iran war, which began in late February with joint U.S. and Israeli strikes. He has acknowledged that the conflict was partially to blame for Republican losses in last week’s midterm elections, while Vice President JD Vance said it was the “real reason” for the GOP rout. The war between Russia and Ukraine also has seen no resolution despite Trump’s repeated statements during his presidential campaign and since taking office that it would end soon. The president suggested earlier this year that his administration would get involved in Cuba. He said in February, for example, that U.S. talks with Havana could lead to a “friendly takeover.” NBC News reported in May that Trump had grown frustrated at the time that the Cuban government was holding on to power despite months of sustained U.S. pressure.

articles.title: Will Democrats try to strip US-Israel initiative from Pentagon funding?
articles.summary: Midterm gains give party room to overhaul NDAA funding, including provision to integrate US-Israeli military industries.
articles.body:
Washington, DC – After a commanding performance in the United States midterm elections, advocates say Democrats are uniquely positioned to strip a controversial measure from a Pentagon funding bill that would codify integration of the US and Israeli military industries.

Earlier this year, Democratic leadership had already opposed the Fiscal Year 2027 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), a sprawling $1.15 trillion package that, along with supplemental bills, includes funding for much of President Donald Trump’s military wishlist, including the “Golden Dome” missile shield and his so-called “Trump-class” battleship plan.

Top party officials, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, had attached their opposition to the Trump administration’s war with Iran and wider affordability issues facing US citizens. Advocates say the leadership must also send the message that the US-Israeli defence production integration is a non-starter.

The current Senate version of the bill, under Section 219, calls for the creation of a so-called “United States-Israel Defense Technology Cooperation Initiative” that would “expand and accelerate bilateral defense technology research, development, testing, evaluation, coordination, and industrial cooperation”.

Cavan Kharrazian, senior policy adviser at Demand Progress, told Al Jazeera that “Democrats need to make it clear right now that their votes for the NDAA depend on substantial changes, including US-Israeli military integration and Iran war prohibition”.

Opposition to Pentagon funding has historically been politically fraught, with lawmakers wary of appearing to not support the US military. But while a version of the funding package passed the Republican-controlled House of Representatives in May, Democrats delayed the Senate version via a procedural vote in July.

They now face a December 11 deadline when current stopgap funding ends, meaning they would need to pass another stopgap measure or the full NDAA to maintain Pentagon funding.

Because the NDAA requires 60 votes to pass, Democrats can exercise outsized leverage in the remaining days of this congressional session, Kharrazian explained. Republicans, meanwhile, face a ticking clock before Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress in January.

“[Democrats] have the leverage to filibuster the NDAA until these provisions are stripped out and they need to commit to blocking NDAA consideration until those changes are secured,” Kharrazian said.

“An amendment vote alone is insufficient if Democrats then let the bill advance with the provisions intact.”

To be sure, Democrats, eager to show they are delivering on voter affordability concerns, have signalled they will seek some overhaul to the current NDAA and related supplemental bills. Defence industry analysts have predicted a major constriction in Pentagon funding, which also includes a stalled $360bn supplemental package.

However, it has been unclear if that would extend to the US-Israeli military development initiative.

“We must push for the development of a more realistic and sustainable approach to our national security – one that does not require a defense budget in excess of $1 trillion or one paid for with draconian cuts to critical domestic programs,” Representative Adam Smith, currently the ranking Democrat on the House Armed Services Committee, said in a statement shortly after the November 3 election results rolled in.

He echoed Schumer, who wrote in a July “dear colleague” letter that Republicans were seeking a Pentagon funding bill “that would dump billions more into the defense industry while long overdue investments in American communities wait”.

Smith had initially supported, but later opposed, the provision to integrate US-Israeli military development. But Schumer and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who are both seeking to retain their leadership positions in their respective chambers, have not publicly stated their positions.

Critics have long warned that the initiative would establish an opaque new avenue for the Pentagon to provide US tax-funded support to Israel via joint development ventures, while dodging congressional oversight. It would also make future policy pivots more difficult, entrenching Israeli-developed technology into US military programmes.

Some have characterised the initiative as the next phase of Washington’s decades-long military support for Israel, with both US and Israeli officials acknowledging direct military aid has become increasingly politically fraught .

“The whole point of Section 219, let’s understand, is to move the US-Israel aid relationship … further outside the purview of Congress, which is to say to sort of inoculate it from democracy,” said Matthew Duss, the executive vice president at the progressive Center for International Policy think tank. “I think Democrats and others who are opposing this measure in the NDAA are on firm ground to hold a hard line.”

“But I think it’ll be tough, especially with this leadership that remains very strongly pro-Israel,” he told Al Jazeera. “I think both Schumer and Jeffries have shown signs they recognise that their respective caucuses are in a very different place ideologically than they are on this issue.”

A growing number of senators have publicly opposed the measure. In July, Senator Chris Van Hollen joined six colleagues in rejecting the provision.

A total of 12 senators have since signed on (PDF) to a new letter released earlier this week, including progressive stalwarts like Bernie Sanders and more centrist figures like Ron Wyden and Tammy Duckworth.

Hamid Bendaas, the communications director for the Institute for Middle East Understanding (IMEU) Policy Project, said the senators represent “a broader range of the Democratic Caucus”.

“So I think that’s a good sign that a good amount of Democrats are ready to really stand against those provisions in the NDAA,” he told Al Jazeera.

Bendaas also pointed to public opinion polls suggesting widespread opposition to US military support for Israel, fuelled by the genocide in Gaza. Both President Trump and Vice President JD Vance have acknowledged that the current state of the US-Israel relationship has become politically fraught.

“I wouldn’t want to be a Democrat or a Republican who votes yes on the text that we’ve seen,” Bendaas said. “For one of the first major bills to pass post-midterms to be a bill that directs the Pentagon to send taxpayer funds to Israel, or, I should say, Israeli companies, some of which are government-owned companies … I think that’s about the worst thing that they could possibly do right now.”

In their letter, the senators wrote the provision would “expand and accelerate the US-Israel defense relationship, including technology sharing, co-production of weapons systems, and bilateral research and development across multiple domains of warfare such as biotechnology, quantum, autonomous systems, artificial intelligence, cyberwarfare, and others”, surpassing integration even with some US NATO allies.

That could, in turn, “threaten US national security interests by handing Israel leverage over American weapons systems and military technology” and “create long-term dependencies by embedding Israeli technology into the US defense industrial base that could make future policy changes costly or difficult to implement”.

“To do so in this instance would be unwise,” the lawmakers wrote. “Especially as the Government of Israel continues to pursue policies in Gaza, the West Bank and other parts of the region that are inconsistent with US interests and values.”

articles.title: The mistake newly-elected Dems admit they can't afford to make with Trump after sweeping 2026 wins
articles.summary: Newly elected Democrats at a Denver conference urged their party to work with Donald Trump on costs and policy rather than focus solely on investigations.
articles.body: DENVER — Congressional Democrats are heading into the next two years with a choice: focus on investigating President Donald Trump and his administration or look for ways to work with him to deliver results for Americans. The party, after sweeping pickups in last week's midterms, right away warned Trump and Republicans to "lawyer up" and in the following days began outlining investigations into the administration, including its handling of immigration enforcement, the president’s business interests and the Justice Department's actions. But newly elected Democrats and strategists at the "What’s Next" conference in Denver told Fox News Digital that their party should seek opportunities to work with Trump. The new guard argues that voters who elected them into office want to see results over partisan fights. ‘LAWYER UP’: DEMS IMMEDIATELY PUT TRUMP ON NOTICE AMID REPUBLICANS' MIDTERM BLOODBATH Hosted by Majority Democrats, the conference brought Democratic leaders, strategists and rising figures together to discuss the party’s direction after the midterms. Organizers billed it as an independent conversation about what Democrats should do next. Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand cautioned his party against making investigations and impeachments the focus of its new political momentum, particularly when the underlying issues have already been reported. Asked what he did not want Democrats to do as they take office, Sand said he did not want to see them "throwing bombs" at Republicans. Voters, he said, need public servants focused on improving their lives. "There are people who are really struggling right now, whose lives have been ruined by high gas prices, by all kinds of policy choices, and they need results," Sand told Fox News Digital. "They need public servants who are actually trying to serve the public." BERNIE SANDERS WARNS DEMOCRATS NOT TO SPEND ALL THEIR TIME INVESTIGATING TRUMP Sand said he questioned the value of investigating matters already covered by the media instead of pursuing work that could help ordinary people. Asked if that meant working with the Trump administration, he said yes. "He’s there, he was put there two years ago. He’s gonna be there another two years," Sand said. "You don’t get to pick and choose who you work with. The people do." Sen.-elect James Talarico, D-Texas, called on Democrats to focus on what they can accomplish now, even as they push for longer-term reforms. "Some of these reforms may not pass until 2029, but the American people cannot wait two years for change," Talarico said. "We must work with President Trump." He urged Democrats to make the Republican president's final two years in office "the most productive of any presidency in American history." Talarico, who became the first Democrat in nearly four decades to win a statewide election in Texas, also warned against getting "bogged down in the same petty fights." "The American people are demanding change, and in this election, they chose our party to deliver it," Talarico said. Democratic strategist Lis Smith offered a related caution, saying the election was "largely a referendum on Donald Trump and less a validation of Democrats and their policies." Smith, a senior advisor for Majority Democrats, said the party still needs to earn voters’ trust and should focus on costs and corruption rather than treating their wins as a mandate for policies they did not campaign on. She also said that Democrats didn't sweep because of their winning message, but rather because fed-up voters cast their ballots as a rebuke of Trump and his policies. "We should not read into these election results as a mandate for far left policies advocated only by a handful of candidates," Smith emphasized. A Reuters/Ipsos poll published this month indicated that nearly three-quarters of Americans wanted Democratic leaders in Congress to make a concerted effort to work with the president.

articles.title: Chris Van Hollen to challenge Chuck Schumer for Senate leadership
articles.summary: Maryland Senator Van Hollen says "new leadership" is needed for Democrats following the party's recent midterm successes.
articles.body:
US Senator Chuck Schumer is facing a challenge to his position as US Senate majority leader from his fellow Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen, as the party prepares to take control of Congress after sweeping the midterm elections.

Van Hollen, 67, said in a post on X on Thursday that Americans voted for change earlier this month and "to deliver, we need new leadership".

Schumer, 75, has led Democrats in the chamber since 2017, serving as both majority and minority leader. He was first elected to the Senate in 1999.

Following the midterms earlier this month, his position has come under pressure by some left-wing Democrats who see him as too moderate and part of the party establishment.

Responding to the challenge, Schumer, who represents New York, said he welcomes "any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead".

He added that he is "proud of what we've accomplished together" in the midterms, and he has "the votes to continue as Democratic leader".

The vote on Senate leader will be held behind closed doors in early December and the winner will assume the role on 4 January, when Democrats take control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives after their midterms successes.

The move by Van Hollen, who represents Maryland, marks the most significant step by a high-profile Democrat to challenge the party's existing leadership following last week's midterms victory.

Announcing his plans to run on X, he wrote that Americans had called on the party to "unrig an economy rigged against working people".

In recent years, Van Hollen has taken positions popular with those on the left of his party.

In 2024, he supported restricting weapons shipments to Israel and criticised the Biden administration over its role in the war in Gaza.

In an interview with MS NOW, Van Hollen - who has served in the Senate for nearly a decade - acknowledged that he is an "underdog" but added that he believes the race is "very much in flux".

Independent Senator Bernie Sanders and Democratic Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed have both publicly come out in support of Van Hollen - while others have also called for new leadership.

In a post on X, Sanders said he believes Van Hollen "will stand up to powerful special interests, take on the billionaire class and fight for working families".

El-Sayed said the challenger would bring "bold leadership" and lead with both "courage and experience".

Others Democrats have publicly backed Schumer.

Senator Jacky Rosen of Nevada said: "He has the experience and the fight to continue leading our diverse caucus at this crucial moment".

Senator Kirsten Gillibrand said: "You will see, despite all the grumblings, enormous gratitude for the hard work he has done to get us to this position."

articles.title: Trump's spy chiefs put Republican leaders on the clock over 'huge priority' as power shift looms over Congress
articles.summary: Trump's intelligence chiefs set a Dec. 9 deadline for Congress to reauthorize FISA Section 702 before Democrats take control of Capitol Hill.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE: President Donald Trump's top administration intelligence officials penned a letter to congressional leaders urging them to reauthorize the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA). An administration official told Fox News Digital the intel measure is at top of mind for the White House to get passed in the still-Republican-controlled Congress before Democrats take a majority on Capitol Hill in January. "This is going to be a huge priority and push by the administration, by the White House for the lame-duck Congress, because this really needs to get done," the administration source said. "Otherwise, we're kind of in trouble from a national security standpoint." They stressed that the White House is "fully on board" with the push by the intelligence agencies' leaders asking Congress to reauthorize the law, including the controversial Section 702. CONGRESS RETURNS TO BRUTAL LAME-DUCK STRETCH WITH SHUTDOWN DEADLINE, LEADERSHIP RACES: 'CLOSET IS FULL OF S—' The letter, signed by Attorney General Todd Blanche, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and CIA Director John Ratcliffe, set a deadline for Dec. 9, 2026, less than a month before the new Congress will be sworn into office. Clayton and Ratcliffe briefed the Gang of 8 — members of Congress who are legally apprised of classified national security matters and covert operations by the executive branch — earlier this week about the status of FISA. TRUMP NOMINATES JAY CLAYTON, FORMER SEC CHAIRMAN, CURRENT US ATTORNEY, AS INTELLIGENCE DIRECTOR "Any delays beyond this date will risk this critical authority lapsing, putting the lives of both Americans in the homeland and our troops stationed abroad at risk in the heightened threat environment briefed to the Gang of 8 earlier this week," the letter says. It is addressed to Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y. SENATE TEMPORARILY EXTENDS NATION’S CONTROVERSIAL SPYING POWERS AFTER HOUSE FUMBLES "As you know, Section 702 is the single most indispensable tool we have to keep our homeland and the American people safe," the letter says. "It enables our Intelligence Community to detect and disrupt terrorist plots, cyber intrusions, and weapons proliferation. No other authority can replace it." FISA's Section 702 has a controversial history. Privacy activists and constitutional scholars have long argued that Section 702 is akin to warrantless surveillance. Under Section 702, intelligence agencies can clandestinely collect the communications of Americans if they are speaking to foreigners who are targets of investigations. The Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) credits Section 702 for thwarting terrorist activities, including a mass casualty terror attack at a Taylor Swift concert in Vienna, Austria, in 2024, and says that 63% of the articles in Trump's daily brief contained FISA Section 702 information reported by the National Security Agency in 2025. JOHNSON FACES GOP REVOLT OVER WARRANTLESS SURVEILLANCE POWERS AHEAD OF KEY VOTE The letter explains that the statutory authority of Section 702 has lapsed, and that collection of such materials will expire on March 16 if FISA is not reauthorized. It goes on to say that the Dec. 9 congressional deadline to begin the renewal process will allow the intelligence agencies the necessary amount of time to complete the steps for continued Section 702 collection before the March expiration date. LAWMAKERS SCRAMBLE AFTER TRUMP DERAILS BID TO REVIVE KEY COUNTERTERRORISM TOOL DAYS AFTER FBI THWARTS UFC PLOT "To prevent a gap in critical intelligence and avoid putting our nation at risk, the government must start the 2027 renewal process by then," the letter states. "If collection stops, we cannot simply turn 702 back on. The Administration looks forward to briefing Congress again in the coming days on the irreplaceable intelligence enabled by Section 702 and the dire risks to our nation if it is allowed to expire." articles.title: Sixth victim confirmed in DC condo-related shooting in US, police say
articles.summary: Police confirm sixth victim in DC condo shooting; suspect dead after barricading himself and starting a fire.
articles.body:
Police have said a sixth person was shot on Thursday morning in Washington, DC , bringing the toll to one person killed and five wounded in an attack they believe was linked to a dispute over maintenance issues in a condo building.

In an updated statement, the Metropolitan Police Department said investigators had found a sixth victim, a woman, after officers initially located five other victims.

She was conscious and breathing with a “non-life-threatening gunshot graze wound”.

“The victim self-treated the wound,” police said.

Two women and two men were taken to hospital, all conscious and breathing.

James Stuart, the 46-year-old manager of the building in which the suspect lived, died at the scene.

Police believe the suspect, a 55-year-old doctor named Matt Wade Lambert, targeted Stuart while Stuart was doing his morning workout at the gym.

The shooting started just before 8am local time (13:00 GMT) at a VIDA Fitness gym in the city’s Logan Circle neighbourhood, about a mile north of the White House.

Police said Lambert shot Stuart inside the gym on the ground floor of the building before going back to his apartment on the seventh floor and firing on people below from his patio.

Five others, some of whom had been working at a construction site across the street. Police have not detailed the circumstances in which the sixth victim was shot.

The shootings unfolded in less than five minutes, according to interim police chief Jeffery Carroll.

Lambert then barricaded himself inside his apartment, where he talked to police negotiators over the phone. Police say he fired at least twice through the door while officers were outside, but no officers were injured.

He also broke the gas line connected to his fireplace and started a fire, which the building’s sprinkler system contained.

Police said Lambert spent most of the conversation with negotiators talking about the dispute with building management.

“Most of the conversation was about the homeowners associations and challenges with that,” said Carroll.

“While our negotiators were communicating with the suspect, they did hear a single gunshot,” he said, adding that Lambert then stopped talking.

When tactical officers forced their way into the apartment, they found him dead from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound.

Police said inside the apartment, they found a shotgun, a rifle, and a handgun, all of which had been used in the shooting.

According to court records cited by The Associated Press, Lambert had filed a lawsuit alleging that he had not been able to enjoy his penthouse since 2024 because of mould, moisture and water problems that began after work had been done on the building’s exterior.

The lawsuit was ongoing, and Lambert appeared to have shared details of the dispute, including photos and an engineering report on an X account called ofMiceandMold.

His lawyer, Joel Braithwaite, told reporters on Thursday that the condo where Lambert had lived since 2017 looked like “a warzone” and that Lambert had spent more than $300,000 on the lawsuit.

articles.title: Incoming GOP congressman backs halting all immigration to US, warns about Sharia law in Texas
articles.summary: Rep.-elect Jace Yarbrough says he favors stopping immigration altogether and repealing the 1965 Hart-Celler Act as he prepares to enter Congress.
articles.body: Rep.-elect Jace Yarbrough, a Republican from Texas, is set to enter Congress on Jan. 3 with an agenda to sharply restrict immigration and preserve what he describes as the "Christian heritage" of the United States, though he doubts the incoming Democratic majorities in both chambers will be willing to work with him. In an interview with Fox News Digital, Yarbrough repeatedly denounced mass migration and said he'd be in favor of "stopping immigration altogether for a time because of how insane this has gotten." He argued the U.S. is admitting far too many immigrants, including individuals he described as "avowedly anti-American" or connected to international terrorist groups. He also said he'd support repealing the 1965 Hart-Celler Act, which abolished the national-origins quota system that favored immigrants from Northern and Western Europe while severely restricting immigration from Asia, Africa and other parts of the world. 'AMERICA FIRST' IMMIGRATION OVERHAUL BILL WOULD CODIFY TRUMP'S CAMPAIGN PROMISES ONCE AND FOR ALL Asked whether he supported restoring national-origin quotas, Yarbrough instead advocated for a merit-based immigration system. Currently, most green cards are issued through family-based immigration, in which U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents sponsor eligible relatives. A much smaller share is issued based on employment qualifications and skills. "You have to justify why it is that you are going to make our country stronger," Yarbrough said. "You have to prove that you want to be a part of this thing. You're going to forswear allegiance to your old country." Yarbrough also expressed concerns about the spread of Sharia law, the Islamic religious legal system that he argued was "completely incompatible" with American values. "We're not thoughtful about whether or not certain cultures are compatible with ours," he said. "My job as a member of Congress ... is to fight for us and be unapologetic about the richness of our history." When asked to provide examples of what he has previously described as the "Islamification of Texas," Yarbrough pointed to a lawsuit filed last year by the East Plano Islamic Center (EPIC), a North Texas mosque. AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI The EPIC mosque is located near Texas' 32nd Congressional District, which Yarbrough will be representing in Congress. "That mosque sued a group of Christian street preachers for preaching the gospel on public sidewalks near the mosque. And that's an example of the kind of anti-American Sharia supremacist behavior, activity, and ideology that I'm talking about," Yarbrough said. In Oct. 2025, the mosque sued Testimonies of God, a Texas-based Baptist ministry, alleging that its members used microphones and bullhorns to disrupt Friday prayer services in violation of the city's noise ordinance. Videos posted to the ministry's social media accounts show its members preaching near the mosque over a period of several months. Plano police records show officers responded to a criminal trespass complaint at the mosque in May, though the log does not identify those involved or indicate whether a citation was issued. A judge dismissed EPIC's lawsuit in March under Texas' anti-SLAPP law, but the mosque appealed, and the case remains pending. TEXAS AG PAXTON SUES EPIC CITY DEVELOPERS AFTER PROBE FINDS ALLEGED FRAUD, MISLEADING MUSLIM-ONLY MARKETING Yarbrough's concerns about EPIC are similar to those of Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, who repeatedly accused the mosque of attempting to establish a community governed by Sharia law. But while Abbott lost his re-election bid to Democrat Gina Hinojosa, Yarbrough won his race with just over 51% of the vote, capturing a seat previously held by a Democrat as his party suffered sweeping losses nationwide. Yarbrough's victory was aided by a 2025 redistricting effort that transformed the 32nd District from a Democratic stronghold into a Republican-leaning seat by adding several conservative rural counties east of Dallas. Yarbrough, however, credited his win to his unwavering embrace of the "America First" agenda, arguing that Republicans should resist calls to moderate despite the party's poor performance in the midterms. DEM WINS TRUMP-TARGETED TEXAS DISTRICT IN REBUKE OF REPUBLICAN REDISTRICTING SHAKEUP He did acknowledge that some of his younger constituents were upset over the Iran war, with some of them expressing frustration that the conflict had contributed to higher gas prices. "I didn't run away from any of the policy convictions of the America First movement," Yarbrough said. "Obviously, that resonated with them because we were one of the few spots where Republicans were able to hold a seat and even gain a seat." Yarbrough, a Stanford-educated attorney, served four years on active duty in the Air Force before transitioning to the reserve in 2015. He currently holds the rank of major and spends about five weeks a year serving at Space Systems Command at Cape Canaveral, Florida. His decision to run for office was driven largely by his belief that the military and institutions where he studied and worked as a lawyer had become increasingly hostile to conservative values. GOP WIPEOUT GOES FROM BAD TO WORSE AS DEMS QUIETLY SCORE ANOTHER MAJOR WIN WITH BIG RAMIFICATIONS The consequences he faced after his refusal to take the COVID-19 vaccine on the "strong advice" of his doctor further pushed him toward a career in politics. That decision earned him a formal reprimand from the Air Force, according to Yarbrough. He also said he resigned from Baker Botts, a prominent Texas law firm, the day before its vaccination policy took effect, which he said would have prevented him from entering the office without proof of vaccination. Baker Botts did not respond to multiple requests for comment from Fox News Digital. "The left just kept coming after me," Yarbrough said. "I finally decided, well, if they're not going to leave me alone, then upon evaluation, maybe it's my job to go and and fight to make them stop." During a candidate forum in February, Yarbrough bluntly said, "I have no interest in representing Democrats," while talking about his vehement disagreement with COVID-19 vaccine mandates employers implemented during the height of the pandemic. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP When asked about those comments, Yarbrough told Fox News Digital that he will represent the people of his district "whether they voted for me or not." Yarbrough argued that many Texans who voted for Democrats were actually Republicans frustrated with their party, rather than supporters of progressive policies he considers extreme. As he prepares to take office, Yarbrough said he was skeptical he'll find much common ground with his fellow Democrats in the House, who will steer the legislative priorities of the chamber for the next two years. "It seems like they're going to be primarily interested in weaponizing, as they have several times in the past, whatever levers of power they've been given to try and go after ... members of the first family and the administration," he said. Still, Yarbrough said he'd be ready to work with anyone who wants to prioritize the interests of American citizens.

articles.title: Feds add D.C. terrorism charge for White House Correspondents’ Dinner gunman
articles.summary: A federal grand jury has added an attempted terrorism charge to the case of Cole Tomas Allen, the man arrested at the White House Correspondent’s Dinner Association dinner in April.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — A federal grand jury has added an attempted terrorism charge to the case of Cole Tomas Allen, the man arrested after he opened fire at the White House Correspondents’ Association Dinner in April. Allen now faces a total of five counts, including a top charge of attempting to assassinate the president of the United States. If convicted, federal prosecutors could potentially seek a federal terrorism sentencing enhancement. Allen previously pleaded not guilty in connection with the April 25 incident. He has not pleaded to the new charge. While there is no federal domestic terrorism statute that broadly outlaws acts of terrorism, Allen has been charged under a local D.C. terrorism law. The same D.C. statute was used against Floyd Fee Corkins, the gunman who was convicted of attacking the Family Research Council in 2012. The office of the U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia is unique in that it prosecutes both federal crimes as well as most local crimes involving adult defendants, so it considers violations of both federal and state laws. The president appoints the head of the office, which is currently led by former judge and Fox News host Jeanine Pirro. Allen, federal prosecutors alleged, “attempted to kill the President of the United States, Donald J. Trump” when he charged through a Secret Service security checkpoint “armed with a 12-gauge pump action shotgun, a .38caliber pistol, multiple knives and daggers, and a significant amount of ammunition.” Trump and Vice President JD Vance were rushed off the stage after Allen charged toward the ballroom at the Washington Hilton where the White House Correspondents’ Dinner was being held. Federal authorities allege that Allen scheduled emails to be sent to his family, friends and former employer explaining his actions. A jury trial has been set for Sept. 7, 2027 before U.S. Judge Trevor N. McFadden. A status conference is scheduled for Dec. 4.

articles.title: Rubio takes aim at 'soulless global bureaucrats' pushing Marxism to undermine America
articles.summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio is delivering a high-profile speech on the "spirit of Marx" Friday at the Federalist Society' National Lawyer's Convention.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: Secretary of State Marco Rubio is taking aim at "soulless global bureaucrats" using "rules-based order" arguments to undermine U.S. foreign policy in a speech Friday, warning that the "spirit of Marx" outlived the Soviet Union. U.S. leaders of both parties defended the "rules-based international order," the network of postwar institutions America built. Rubio is set to argue the system has been turned against the country that built it, the same case he made at his January 2025 confirmation hearing, when he called the postwar order "a weapon being used against us." In a preview of Rubio’s speech obtained by Fox News Digital, he outlines how Marxism still has a strong presence in Western society, a view which is relevant amid the rise of communist and Marxist beliefs that have driven protests against the administration and Western beliefs. The remarks are subject to change during his speech. "For this global elite, 'international law' is not a neutral body of rules," Rubio is expected to say. "It's an instrument to advance their interests under the pretense of universal principles. They’re staunch defenders of democracy, until a particular election challenges their interests." RUBIO PUTS ENTIRE WORLD ON NOTICE AGAINST RISE OF 'POISONOUS' FAR-LEFT TERROR 'MASKED AS EQUALITY' "Even as we defeated the institution of Soviet communism, we did not triumph over the spirit of Marx," Rubio’s expected remarks read. "It lives on, in these new forms and doctrines, which would subordinate the national will to the menial consensus of the world. Marxism, in its traditional expression, sought to abolish the distinctions between men; the radicals of our time seek to abolish the distinctions between nations themselves." Rubio is expected to address the Federalist Society at the National Lawyer’s Convention on Friday to where he will go after the International Criminal Court and other global bodies he says are using the law as a political weapon, not to deliver justice. The secretary of state argues that they're trying to tie America's hands and let unelected judges and bureaucrats overseas override decisions that belong to the American people, according to a State Department source. RUBIO'S CALL TO COMBAT GLOBAL FUNDERS OF FAR-LEFT TERRORISM COULD PUT SINGHAM IN CROSSHAIRS The secretary of state is expected to defend the administration's sanctions on the ICC, which he calls "an unelected world tribunal." If it tries to enforce its "paper decrees" against Americans, he plans to say, the U.S. answer will echo the Roman general Pompey: "Stop quoting laws to men with swords." He also will push back on those who say Americans live on "stolen land," arguing that critics who stand behind this belief deny the nation's right to exist, and cast the U.S. as "a nation of irrepressible ambition," according to the excerpts. REAGAN-ERA OFFICIAL WARNS ‘RED-GREEN ALLIANCE’ HAS SHARED GOAL OF ‘DESTROYING’ AMERICA Last week, Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed invoked "self-determination" and developed an argument about America’s role in the international system created after World War II, calling it a "chief violator" of international law. "The beauty of this country is our ideals," El-Sayed said. "We led the effort in this country to build a rules-based international order," he continued. "We built the United Nations and the World Health Organization and the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court so that we could uphold the ideals of democracy. We did that. And then we proceeded to be the chief violator of exactly those same ideals. To call our country to those ideals became an open question, how could you?" LAWMAKERS RAISE ALARM OVER NEVILLE ROY SINGHAM'S $278M NETWORK SPREADING CCP PROPAGANDA IN THE U.S. El-Sayed’s words echoed language used late last year by Neville Roy Singham, whose financial network has supported CodePink and other left-wing organizations. After his wedding to Evans in 2017 and the sale of ThoughtWorks, the technology company he founded, Singham directed $285 million to nonprofits and media organizations, according to a Fox News Digital investigation. The People’s Forum received $22.4 million from Singham, while CodePink received $1.33 million. BreakThrough BT Media Inc., which operates BreakThrough News, received $1.098 million, according to tax filings. Singham and his wife, CodePink co-founder Jodie Evans, live in Shanghai, China. In a speech exactly one year ago, on Nov. 13, 2025, to the "Global South Academic Forum" at the Golden Tulip Hotel in Shanghai, Singham argued that the existing "international rules-based order" was built on a false narrative of World War II and called for a "new world order" based on multilateralism advanced by Chinese President Xi Jinping and the Communist Party of China. JIM BANKS, GOP LAWMAKERS RALLY BEHIND DOJ PROBE INTO ALLEGED CCP-LINKED FUNDING NETWORK "The international rules-based order was created by another lie," Singham said. "If we want to therefore have a new world order that is based on the multilateralism that President Xi and CPC and China have proposed, we have to undo the ideological damage that has been done by the narrative of World War II," Singham had said. RUBIO SANCTIONS CUBAN GROUPS WITH TIES TO US NONPROFIT NETWORK FUNDED BY COMMUNIST DONOR NEVILLE ROY SINGHAM This hostility to the U.S. has infused itself in the anti-American work of far-left organizations. At the People's Forum, Tricontinental and other groups funded by Singham the programming includes Cuba solidarity campaigns, Venezuela advocacy, anti-Iran sanctions initiatives, opposition to NATO expansion and educational events on China, all framed within a broader narrative of "resistance" to U.S. influence. Event flyers and social media posts repeatedly highlight Cuba, promoting teach-ins, cultural programming and delegations opposing U.S. policy. That narrative aligns with Singham’s rejection of the Western system. Fox News Digital investigations have found that the "spirit of Marx" has storefronts, syllabi, fundraising apparatus in America’s nonprofit world and a critical role as the conduit for sending foot soldiers into America’s streets for protests to defend communist regimes across the world and promulgate anti-American propaganda. US BASES, ICE FACILITIES TARGETED IN CUBA-LINKED 24-HOUR ACTIVIST MOBILIZATION PLAN At the People’s Forum in Manhattan, its 1804 Books bookstore and press describes itself as a source of "socialist literature and revolutionary theory," selling books by Marx, including a coloring book for children. Fox News Digital’s investigation traced $22.44 million to the People’s Forum and $16.76 million to Tricontinental through Neville Roy Singham’s funding network. The bookstore’s catalog offers a reading list for that worldview: Marx’s Critique of the Gotha Program, his Critique of Political Economy and The German Ideology, written with philosopher Friedrich Engels. Within the Singham network, Tricontinental places Marxism in its institutional purpose. Its statement of mission and work identifies "national liberation Marxism" as its anchoring tradition and invokes Marx’s argument that philosophy should change the world. The "Marxist Education Project" says it operates through the tax-exempt Movement Education Project Group Inc., and embraces Marxism as its framework. The People’s Forum once hosted its Capital, Volume II study group. The "People Before Profits Education Fund," also known as the Chelsea Fund for Education, solicits support for "Marxist education" and lists the "Little Red Schoolhouse," a national Marxist school training young activists, among its projects. Lutnick in hot seat over Nvidia-Megaspeed scandal

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is facing heat in Washington over his stance on AI chip export controls following Nvidia’s national security scandal this week.

Lutnick is under scrunity after reports emerged this week that he took a softer line on Nvidia over the tech giant’s AI chip sales to China and failed to put the Singaporean firm Megaspeed on the trade entity blacklist.

In the face of calls to testify from both sides of the aisle, Lutnick agreed to appear before Congress, but the blame game is already starting with the Trump administration.

“Treasury, War, USTR [U.S. Trade Representative] and State … were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Friday on CNBC’s “Squawk Box.”

“But Commerce has the pen. Commerce BIS has the pen, and you will have to ask them about their internal processes,” Bessent added, referring to Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security.

Megaspeed is at the center of the Nvidia scandal, an ordeal that led the company’s founder, Jensen Huang , to resign as CEO on Thursday .

Reports indicate Huang had an affair with a former Megaspeed executive whom U.S. intelligence officials believe may be a Chinese spy.

It’s not clear when Trump administration officials were made aware of the intelligence community’s suspicions, but Bessent’s comments signal the administration was aware of risks involving Megaspeed.

Marshall Billingslea , who worked at the Treasury Department during Trump’s first term, noted it is “quite unusual” for Bessent to go public about Cabinet-level discussions about “a matter as sensitive as” the Nvidia-Megaspeed affair.

“To his credit, Scott Bessent & [Secretary of State Marco] Rubio’s team have consistently been right on this topic. Lutnick just ran roughshod over everyone,” Billingslea wrote on the social platform X.

articles.title: Jeffries outlines Democratic plans for Medicare expansion
articles.summary: House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (N.Y.) on Friday endorsed efforts to lower the Medicare eligibility age and expand the program, as Democrats try to navigate internal tensions around a progressive push for “Medicare for All.” During a conference in Denver about the future of the Democratic Party, Jeffries outlined the healthcare legislative priorities Democrats plan…
articles.body:
House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (N.Y.) on Friday endorsed efforts to lower the Medicare eligibility age and expand the program, as Democrats try to navigate internal tensions around a progressive push for “Medicare for All.”

During a conference in Denver about the future of the Democratic Party, Jeffries outlined the healthcare legislative priorities Democrats plan to tackle once he takes over as House Speaker in January.

Jeffries said the party must first undo Republican cuts to Medicaid funding and restore the Affordable Care Act’s temporary enhanced premium tax credits that Democrats provided during the COVID-19 pandemic.

While he stopped short of endorsing Medicare for All, Jeffries said Democrats need to go further than merely restoring what Republicans took.

“I think we’ve got to lower the age of eligibility as it relates to Medicare. I think we’ve got to make sure that we cover hearing, vision and dental, and we’ve got to make sure that every child in America can be able to see a doctor with high-quality affordable healthcare,” Jeffries said.

Medicare for All has become a critical issue on the left over the last decade, largely because of the efforts of Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.).

Buoyed by the victories of candidates like Abdul El-Sayed (D) in Michigan, progressives in the House and Senate are expected to make a significant push for single-payer healthcare.

After the election, Sanders called on Democrats to lower the Medicare age to 55 through budget reconciliation, which can pass on a party-line vote, as an “immediate first step” toward Medicare for All.

Sanders also said Democrats should add dental, vision and hearing coverage to Medicare and expand children’s coverage.

Jeffries, who has been criticized by progressive activists for not being bold enough and for being friendly to special interests, was repeatedly heckled by protesters in Denver.

“Why should we trust you?” one shouted, while another called Jeffries a “traitor.”

But unlike his Senate counterpart, Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), Jeffries faces no serious competition in his bid to be elected House Speaker.

“Remember y’all, I grew up in Brooklyn,” he said with a smile.
